 Article
 A Portable UV-LED/RGB Sensor for Real-Time Bacteriological
Water Quality Monitoring Using ML-Based MPN Estimation
Andrés Saavedra-Ruiz 1 and Pedro J. Resto-Irizarry 1,2, *
 1 Bioengineering Graduate Program, University of Puerto Rico Mayagüez, Mayagüez, PR 00680, USA;
andres.saavedra@upr.edu 2 Mechanical Engineering Department, University of Puerto Rico Mayagüez, Mayagüez, PR 00680, USA
 * Correspondence: pedroj.resto@upr.edu
 Abstract: Bacteriological water quality monitoring is of utmost importance for safeguard-
ing public health against waterborne diseases. Traditional methods such as membrane
filtration (MF), multiple tube fermentation (MTF), and enzyme-based assays are effective in
detecting fecal contamination indicators, but their time-consuming nature and reliance on
specialized equipment and personnel pose significant limitations. This paper introduces a
novel, portable, and cost-effective UV-LED/RGB water quality sensor that overcomes these
challenges. The system is composed of a multi-well self-loading microfluidic device for
sample-preparation-free analysis, RGB sensors for data acquisition, UV-LEDs for excitation,
and a portable incubation system. Commercially available defined substrate technology,
most probable number (MPN) analysis, and machine learning (ML) are combined for the
real-time monitoring of bacteria colony-forming units (CFU) in a water sample. Fluores-
cence signals from individual wells are captured by the RGB sensors and analyzed using
Multilayer Perceptron Neural Network (MLPNN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM)
algorithms, which can quickly determine if individual wells will be positive or negative by
the end of a 24 h period. The novel combination of ML and MPN analysis was shown to
predict in 30 min the bacterial concentration of a water sample with a minimum prediction
accuracy of 84%.
 Keywords: water quality (WQ); defined substrate test (DST); most probable number (MPN);
machine learning (ML); point-of-care
 1. Introduction
 Waterborne diseases pose a significant threat to public health, leading to an annual
occurrence of 7.15 million cases and 6630 deaths in the United States alone [ 1 ]. This includes
diseases such as cholera, typhoid fever, hepatitis, gastrointestinal ailments, and respiratory
tract infections, often originating from pathogenic microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses,
fungi, and intestinal worms. As a result, monitoring water quality is indispensable for
safeguarding public health and preserving ecological equilibrium [2,3].
Effective water quality analysis depends on measuring various parameters. While
traditional physico-chemical indicators like the potential of hydrogen (pH), electrical
conductivity (EC), turbidity (Turb), total dissolved solids (TDS), total phosphorus (TPh),
total nitrogen (TNit), and dissolved oxygen (DO) offer insights into water quality [ 4 ], they
do not directly reflect potential health or agricultural implications. The detection of bacteria,
including total coliforms, Escherichia coli ( E. coli ), and Enterococcus faecalis ( E. faecalis ), is one
of the most used metrics for assessing bacteriological contamination [ 5 ]. These indicators,
characterized by distinct biochemical traits, serve as reliable markers to determine the
 Biosensors 2025 , 15 , 284 https://doi.org/10.3390/bios15050284\n\n---\n\n## Page 85\n\nBiosensors 2025 , 15 , 284 2 of 17
suitability of water and food for human consumption [ 6 ]. The geometric mean (GM) and
statistical threshold value (STV), measured in colony-forming units (CFU) per 100 mL, are
the statistical values used in bacteriological water quality standards. The 2012 Recreational
Water Quality Criteria (2012 RWQC) recommends thresholds of 35 CFU per 100 mL GM for
marine and freshwater enterococci and 126 CFU per 100 mL GM for E. coli in freshwater [ 7 ].
Similarly, the Beach Action Value (BAV) defines limits of 70 CFU per 100 mL for marine
and freshwater enterococci and 235 CFU per 100 mL for E. coli in freshwater [7].
Established methods such as multitube fermentation (MTF) and membrane filtration
(MF) are often viewed as the gold standard for assessing water quality. These techniques
are supported by standardized and accredited protocols that facilitate inter-laboratory
comparisons. However, they present drawbacks, including the need for cold transporta-
tion, trained personnel, laboratory space and equipment, expensive consumables, and
a minimum 24 h incubation period for obtaining results. Alternative methods include
molecular and enzyme-based techniques, which mitigate some of these drawbacks and
offer significantly faster detection [ 8 , 9 ]. The defined substrate technology (DST) method,
exemplified by Colilert TM and Enterolert TM (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc., Westbrook, ME,
USA), uses enzyme-substrate fluorescence to quantify total coliforms, E. coli , and entero-
cocci [ 10 , 11 ]. This EPA-approved approach is easier to use than traditional methods and
features a streamlined process, although it may involve human error during quantification.
The IDEXX Quanti-Tray/2000 (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc., Westbrook, ME, USA) divides
a 100 mL sample into 97 wells of two different sizes and uses the most probable number
(MPN) method to determine the bacterial count in the original sample [ 11 ]. However, like
MTF and MF, DST requires specialized laboratory equipment and cold transportation, and
it has an incubation time of 24 h per test.
Recent advancements in sensor technology have introduced alternative methods to
accelerate bacterial detection. For instance, the Colifast ALARM TM , developed by the
Norwegian company Colifast (Colifast AS, Lysaker, Norway), automates detection and
reduces the time to detection by using DST and focusing on the presence of fluorescence
due to bacterial growth. The system collects and incubates water samples in a specialized
chamber connected to a detector. The substrate 4-methylumbelliferyl- ω -D-glucuronide is
used for detecting E. coli , while 4-methylumbelliferyl- ω -D-galactoside is used for detecting
total coliforms [ 12 , 13 ]. However, a disadvantage of this system is that it requires installation
in a fixed setting, limiting its use in field applications and potentially increasing the
operational costs due to the need for dedicated space and technical oversight. Additionally,
the company has developed the Colifast Field Kit, which enables measurements within
75 min to 2 h and is more cost-effective than the standard version. However, its detection
limits are tailored to concentrations above 500 CFU per 100 mL. However convenient, many
of these systems require investments between thousands to tens of thousands of dollars.
These systems use ultraviolet (UV) light and fluorescence as indicators of the presence
of bacteria.
Ultraviolet and color light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and RGB sensors can serve as low-
cost alternatives to traditional water quality monitoring equipment. UV light has ubiquitous
applications in bioengineering, including sterilization, phototherapy, the activation of
photosensitive compounds, and microscopy. In the field of water quality, ultraviolet–
visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy has been used to measure parameters such as chemical
oxygen demand, heavy metal ions, nitrate-nitrogen, and dissolved organic carbon. These
precise measurements are essential to ensure the safety of drinking water and preserve
ecological balance [ 14 ]. Other examples include the combination of UV-Vis and fluorescence
spectroscopy to enable real-time detection of biological and chemical contaminants [ 15 ].
Zhang et al. employed UV-Vis spectrometry combined with artificial neural networks\n\n---\n\n## Page 86\n\nBiosensors 2025 , 15 , 284 3 of 17
to evaluate key water quality parameters, including total organic carbon (TOC), total
suspended solids (TSS), and chemical oxygen demand (COD), underscoring its potential
for real-time water quality assessment [ 16 ]. Lyu and Zhao present the development of
statistical regression models and artificial neural networks to estimate concentrations
of nitrogen, phosphorus, COD, and suspended solids in eutrophic rivers using UV-Vis
spectroscopy, concluding that these models demonstrate a high level of accuracy and
reliability in predicting water quality parameters [17].
RGB sensors have been applied to monitor different parameters related to water quality.
Parra et al. developed, calibrated, and tested a low-cost optical sensor for measuring and
classifying water turbidity using an RGB LED in combination with a photoresistor. The data
collected were then analyzed using machine learning models determining turbidity with
an accuracy of 91.23% when employing the K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm [18]. Similarly,
Sampedro and Salgueiro incorporate red, green, blue, and infrared light sources with a
photoresistor to enable remote turbidity measurements in aquatic environments without
the need for complex analytical equipment [ 19 ]. Benavides et al. demonstrated the use
of low-cost RGB sensors for monitoring microalgae growth in a photobioreactor. The
sensor was calibrated using a commercial spectrophotometer for offline measurements
and a submerged electrode for real-time, online monitoring. This research highlights the
significance of monitoring and process control in microalgae production, with applications
extending to biofuels, pigments, cosmetics, animal feed, and wastewater treatment [ 20 ].
Pazzi et al. used TCS3200 RGB sensors with an Arduino microcontroller and microfluidic
paper-based analytical devices ( μ PADs) for measuring pH, showing high accuracy and
alignment with values obtained from a traditional pH meter [ 21 ]. In contrast to the scientific
literature, the approach presented in this manuscript is, to the author’s knowledge, the
first to integrate UV excitation LEDs and RGB sensors in an acrylic microfluidic device for
bacteriological water quality measurements.
Microfluidic devices can be integrated with excitation LEDs and fluorescence sensors
and can offer low-cost, portable, and automated capture and analysis of small volumes.
Lab-on-a-chip sensors have been developed for water quality monitoring, specifically
for detecting microorganisms, heavy metals, organic compounds, and various other sub-
stances [ 22 ]. Recent research has led to the development of microfluidic-based technologies
that enable the monitoring of multiple water contaminants with precision comparable
to traditional methods while significantly reducing detection times. In one such study,
Gowda et al. designed a microfluidic device capable of capturing water samples, lysing
bacterial cells, extracting nucleic acids, and quantifying bacteria using a droplet digital
loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay. This portable system can quickly detect
bacteria like E. faecalis directly on-site, completing the entire test in just 1 h and requiring
less than 5 min of manual sample handling [23].
Additional innovations aimed at reducing the detection time for E. faecalis have in-
cluded recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) combined with a lateral flow assay
(LFA). This method allows for testing within approximately 30 min, a significant reduction
compared to the 24 h required by the Enterolert™ (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc., Westbrook,
ME, USA) test. However, the RPA-LFA approach compromises sensitivity, detecting E. fae-
calis with 10 to 1000 times lower efficiency compared to Enterolert™ [ 24 ]. This highlights
the ongoing challenge of developing low-cost technologies that are both rapid and sensitive
enough for effective water quality monitoring.
To accelerate the detection of bacteria in water, machine learning (ML) can be used
with lab-on-a-chip concepts to efficiently capture, monitor, and store water samples. As a
branch of artificial intelligence (AI), ML involves creating algorithms that enable computers
to learn from data and enhance their performance over time [ 25 , 26 ]. By developing mathe-\n\n---\n\n## Page 87\n\nBiosensors 2025 , 15 , 284 4 of 17
matical models that identify patterns and relationships within datasets, ML can predict the
behavior of new data, making it an effective tool for real-time water quality monitoring.
Paepae et al. examined the most used parameters and machine learning (ML) algorithms
in water quality research. They identified four predominant algorithms: neural networks
(NN), random forest (RF), multiple linear regression (MLR), and support vector machines
(SVM) [ 4 ]. Neural networks were favored for their ability to model complex nonlinear
relationships in water quality data, making them highly suitable for tasks requiring high
predictive accuracy [ 27 ]. Random Forest gained popularity for its robustness, capacity
to handle large datasets with high dimensionality, and effectiveness in reducing overfit-
ting [ 28 , 29 ]. The multiple linear regression (MLR) facilitates hypothesis testing and model
selection. To enhance reliability and consistency, steps such as multicollinearity diagnostics,
cross-validation, and regularization are conducted prior to model development. In water
quality index (WQI) modeling, MLR integrates multiple physicochemical parameters into a
single score that represents overall water quality [ 30 ]. The Support Vector Machine (SVM)
algorithm works well with small datasets but can face computational efficiency issues with
larger ones. Conversely, limited sample sizes may not sufficiently capture classification
features. Effective data streamlining is essential to preserve support vectors and maintain
data integrity [31].
In this study, rapid prototyping and open-source tools are used to create a water quality
sensor with a microfluidic device and everything necessary to carry out and quantify a DST
assay at the point-of-care. MPN quantification occurs by observing the number of positive
(fluorescing) wells in the microfluidic device. Each well is loaded with the Enterolert™
substrate mixed with bacteria-containing water and placed within a portable incubation
system. The system uses UV light excitation and RGB sensors to monitor the water samples
in each well, generating a dataset to train two machine learning algorithms: multilayer
perceptron neural networks (MLPNN) and support vector machine (SVM). Once trained,
the ML can quickly predict whether a well will be positive or negative after the 24 h period.
In conjunction with the MPN table, this technique predicts the water sample MPN in a few
hours using low-cost, open-source materials.
 2. Materials and Methods
 2.1. Microfluidic Device Design and Loading
 The microfluidic device was designed to facilitate both sample handling and the most
probable number (MPN) quantification of bacteria. The microfluidic device was constructed
from four acrylic sheets, including a base sheet without apertures, two intermediate sheets,
each featuring eight wells with channels for fluid movement, and a top sheet solely for fluid
inlets/outlets (Figure 1a). The dimensions of each acrylic sheet measured 50 mm → 100 mm ,
and the wells possessed a diameter of 16 mm (Figure 1b). Inlet and outlet ports connect to
each well through channels of 500 μ m height, h ; 3.175 mm width, w ; and 22 mm length,
 L , respectively. L was taken as the distance between the inlet and outlet ports. The device
was fabricated using 3.175 mm cast acrylic sheets and an Epilog 60W CO 2 laser cutter
(Figure 1c). The CO 2 laser cutter operated at 25% speed and 85% power. Double-sided
medical-grade adhesive (ARcare ® 90106, Adhesives Research, Inc., Glen Rock, PA, USA)
was used to bond the four acrylic layers. The microfluidic device was designed to fill
with liquid passively by comparing the approximate hydraulic resistance of the channels
 ( R Hyd = ( 12 η L ) / ( 1 ↑ 0.63
 ( h w
 )
 h 3 w ) to the hydrostatic pressure ( P Hyd = ρ gL ) provided
at the channel inlet when submerged. A comparison is shown in Figure 1d where P Hyd
 is the hydrostatic inlet pressure, and ∆ P represents the pressure necessary to overcome
the hydraulic resistance of the channel, ∆ P = QR Hyd , assuming a volumetric flow rate Q

In the experiments, 108 mL of distilled water and a lyophilized E. faecalis pellet
( Enterococcus faecalis WDCM Vitroids™, Sigma-Aldrich Co. LLC, St. Louis, MO, USA)
hydrated in 2 mL of PBS were used. The IDEXX Enterolert™ (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc.,
Westbrook, ME, USA) reagent was then added to the 110 mL solution and was thoroughly
shaken to ensure homogeneity. The microfluidic device was filled with 10 mL of this mix,
while 100 mL was used to fill the IDEXX Quanti-Tray/2000. The inlets and outlets of the
microfluidic device were sealed with polyester film PET tape and incubated for 24 h in a
portable platform. The Quanti-Tray/2000 was incubated for 24 h in an incubator oven at
41 ↓ C.
 2.2. Portable Temperature-Controlled Incubation and UV-LED/RGB Excitation and Emission
System for Bacterial Detection
 Achieving the required incubation temperature of 41 ↓ C for a 24 h period is vital for
accurate results. A temperature control system was developed using a Peltier thermoelectric
cooler (Digi-key Electronics, TEC-12706, Thief River Falls, MN, USA) as the heating element,
a copper sheet to distribute heat, and a thermistor (Einstronic, MF52AT, Kota Kinabalu,
Malaysia) as the temperature sensor. These components are controlled by an Arduino
Nano 33 IoT (Digi-key Electronics, part ABX00027, MN, USA), which interfaces with the
Peltier cell via a motor drive module (Einstronic, MX1508, Kota Kinabalu, Malaysia). A
customized case was designed in Solid Works and fabricated using a 3D printer (Creality
CR 10S, Shenzhen, China) and holds the Peltier cell, copper sheet, and microfluidic device,
Figure 2a. Figure 2b presents the temperature response of the system with and without a
control system (CS), demonstrating the effectiveness of the control system in stabilizing
temperature fluctuations.

The UV-LED/RGB system combines RGB sensors (Adafruit Industries LLC, TCS34725,
New York, NY, USA) with 365 nm wavelength UV LEDs (Digi-key Electronics, part 1497-
1479-1-ND, MN, USA), all controlled by the Arduino Nano 33 IoT. Originally designed with
an LED emitter, the RGB sensors were calibrated using various color sheets (white, black,
red, green, and blue). UV LEDs are then integrated into the RGB sensor system to enable
fluorescence detection in water samples, Figure 2c. The combination of the RGB sensors and
UV-LEDs is named the UV-LED/RGB system. To enhance accuracy and minimize noise, a
black acrylic layer is incorporated into the RGB system as a filter, effectively reducing UV
light scattering (Figure 2d).
The UV-LED/RGB system is designed with a temperature control unit at the base,
where the microfluidic device is inserted. The RGB sensor monitoring system is positioned
in the upper section, Figure 3a. These RGB sensors communicate with the microcontroller
using I2C communication protocol, with a multiplexer (Texas Instruments, TCA9548A,
Dallas, TX, USA) enabling simultaneous communication with up to eight RGB sensors.
Data could be viewed in real time through either wired or wireless connections. A com-
prehensive database was constructed, incorporating clear, red, green, and blue signals for
each sensor, yielding a total of thirty-two columns of data used as inputs in the machine
learning algorithms.

inoculated with a 50–80 CFU pellet. The IDEXX Quanti-Tray/2000 was used as a benchmark
and measured a bacterial concentration of 35 CFU/100 mL, while the UV-LED/RGB system

and serves to confirm the growth detected by the UV-LED/RGB system.
For this study, 11 experimental tests were conducted, distributed as follows: 4 tests
with concentrations ranging from 50 to 80 CFU, 3 tests from 80 to 120 CFU, 1 test from 130
to 300 CFU, 1 test from 3k to 7k CFU (undiluted), 1 test from 50k to 150k CFU (undiluted),
and 1 test from 50k to 150k CFU (diluted 1:1000).

 Two machine learning (ML) algorithms, support vector machine (SVM) and multilayer
perceptron neural networks (MLPNN), were selected for this study due to their widespread
application in water quality analysis. Equation (3) applies the first derivative to the RGB
sensor signals, denoted as c for clear, r for red, g for green, and b for blue. This transfor-

their performance.

The SVM algorithm was developed in Python version 3.8.8, an open-source software,
using a combination of ML and data manipulation libraries such as NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-
Learn, TensorFlow, and Keras. A normalized and derivative-transformed dataset (using
Equation (3)) includes measurements from 8 UV-LED/RGB sensors, with inputs for each
sensor representing values for clear, red, green, and blue, both in their original and derived
forms. The dataset is divided into training and testing sets with a 70:30 ratio using Scikit-
Learn’s train_test_split function. The SVM model is fitted with a polynomial kernel, with
tuned parameters (C = 100, gamma = ‘scale’, coef0 = 0.5, degree = 4), to capture nonlinear
relationships in the data. The model’s performance is evaluated using metrics such as
accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, represented by Equations (4)–(7) [ 33 ], where TP
stands for true positives, TN for true negatives, FP for false positives, and FN for false
negatives. These metrics are visualized for each sensor using bar graphs, and the results
are plotted using Matplotlib version 3.7.5 to generate detailed graphs of each sensor’s
performance. The flowchart of the SVM algorithm is shown on the right-hand side of

 ing rate, with regularization parameter alpha set to 0.001, and the maximum number of

 score (Equations (4)–(7), respectively) [33], which are visualized for each sensor using bar
 graphs, ensuring robust model development. A plotting stage was also included to visu-
 alize the predicted and actual values, demonst rating the model’s ability to generalize
 across different datasets. The flowchart of the MLPNN algorithm is shown on the left-
 hand side of Figure 4.

 3. Results and Discussion
 3.1. UV-LED/RGB System
 Several experiments were conducted using the UV-LED/RGB system, comparing its
results with those obtained from the IDEXX Quanti-Tray/2000 system. The experiments\n\n---\n\n## Page 93\n\nBiosensors 2025 , 15 , 284 10 of 17
were carried out using different concentrations of bacteria to assess the performance of the
UV-LED/RGB system. Figure 5a shows “clear” color channel signals from sensor number 4
for experiments with different bacterial concentrations: 37.6, 110.9, and >166.4 CFU/100 mL.
All curves exhibit the characteristic sigmoidal behavior of bacterial growth, confirming
the system’s ability to monitor bacterial growth in real time. It can be observed that as
the bacterial concentration increases, the growth curve’s slope becomes steeper, and the
exponential phase begins earlier.

 Figure 5. ( a ) UV-LED/RGB sensor number 4 “clear” color channel showing sigmoidal bacteria growth
curves for different concentrations of bacteria in water samples. ( b ) Normalized RGB signals from the

Figure 5b illustrates the normalized RGBC signals from an experiment with a bacterial
concentration of 37.6 CFU. Wells 0, 1, and 5 demonstrated a positive response to the pres-
ence of bacteria, as indicated by their sigmoidal trends throughout the incubation period,
unlike the other wells. This figure provides a clear example of monitoring low bacterial
concentrations in water, adhering to the EPA BAV standards for recreational activities
(37.6 CFU/100 mL). The exponential phase for wells 1 and 5 occurs at approximately 12 h
into the incubation period, suggesting that this duration is necessary to detect bacterial
presence. In contrast, well 0 required more than 20 h to reach the exponential phase,\n\n---\n\n## Page 94\n\nBiosensors 2025 , 15 , 284 11 of 17
highlighting that solely interpreting sensor signals might not be sufficient for accurately
determining bacterial concentrations in water samples within the first 12 h.
Figure 5c presents the first derivative of the normalized signals from the same experi-
ment, highlighting the same wells, 0, 1, and 5, as positive. Applying the first derivative to
the normalized data serves as an alternative method to determine contamination in wells.
It also helps in reducing the detection time of bacterial growth in the wells because the
positive slope of the exponential phase first derivative can easily be distinguished from
the flat curves of non-fluorescing wells. The first derivative data also provides additional
information to the ML algorithms for predicting wells with bacterial contamination.
The UV-LED/RGB system was benchmarked against the IDEXX Quanti-Tray/2000
using lyophilized pellets of different CFU concentrations, as shown in Table 1. The UV-
LED/RGB system presents a smaller detection range of 10.7 to 166.4 CFU versus the Quanti-
Tray/2000’s range of 1 to 2419 CFU. The UV-LED/RGB system showed lower accuracy,
with an average of 55.9 CFU (STD 31.7 CFU) when using 50–80 CFU pellets, compared
to 37.2 CFU (STD 4.0 CFU) for the Quanti-Tray/2000. The UV-LED/RGB and Quanti-
Tray/2000 systems detected averages of 81.6 CFU (STD 64.4 CFU) and 82.1 CFU (STD
8.5 CFU) when using 80–120 CFU pellets, respectively. When using 130–300 CFU pellets,
the UV-LED/RGB system reported 110.9 CFU versus 165.8 CFU for the Quanti-Tray/2000.
Both systems accurately detected concentrations exceeding their upper detection limits.
When using 3–7K CFU and 50–150K CFU pellets, the UV-LED/RGB reported >166.4 CFU,
while the Quanti-Tray/2000 reported >2419.6 CFU. Overall, results from the UV-LED/RGB
system are consistent with the Quanti-Tray/2000, but it suffers from larger margins of error
than the benchmark. The measurements obtained from the UV-LED/RGB may not always
be the same as the Quanti-Tray/2000, but the reference results fall within the confidence
intervals shown in Figure 1e.

 3.2. Machine Learning Algorithms
 The database for the ML algorithms is divided into 70% for the training stage and 30%
for the testing stage. Initially, the full 24 h of data from each experiment are used to develop
the model. The database for the 24 h period consists of 47,402 data points, with 33,181 (70%)
allocated for the training stage and 14,221 (30%) for the testing stage. During the training
stage, the output variable, or target, is defined by assigning a “0” for the absence of bacteria
in the well and a “1” for the presence of bacteria. Subsequently, the database is restricted to
the lag phase in the experimental data, allowing the ML algorithms to analyze this phase
with the aim of reducing the detection time.
Figure 6a,b illustrates the confusion matrix for each sensor when using the SVM and
MLPNN algorithms, respectively, providing a visual representation of performance in\n\n---\n\n## Page 95\n\nBiosensors 2025 , 15 , 284 12 of 17
terms of correct and incorrect classifications. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC)
curves for both models are presented in Figure 6c,d, highlighting each algorithm’s dis-
criminative capability through their respective areas under the curve (AUC). The graphs
comparing accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score metrics between the algorithms are dis-
played in Figure 6e,f , emphasizing the performance differences between SVM and MLPNN.
Figure 6g,h presents the metrics in tabular form alongside the execution times for each
algorithm, offering a concise and comparative summary of their efficiency and effectiveness.

Upon analyzing Figure 6g,h, it becomes evident that the performance of the MLPNN
and SVM algorithms was evaluated across several sensors, with both demonstrating
high effectiveness in data classification, consistently achieving strong metrics in accuracy,
precision, recall, and F1 score. However, the comparative analysis reveals subtle differences
between the two models. MLPNN exhibited more consistent performance, achieving
perfect or near-perfect metrics across most sensors, including sensors 4, 6, and 0, where it
achieved exceptional results with values of 1.00 or 0.99 in all metrics. On the other hand,
SVM also showed excellent performance, achieving perfect metrics in sensors 5, 1, and 2.
Nevertheless, it experienced a slight decline in performance on other sensors, particularly
on Sensor 6, where the metrics dropped to 0.94. Sensors 7 and 3 exhibited slightly lower
metrics with the SVM algorithm, reaching values of 0.97. This variability suggests that
while SVM is robust, it may face more challenges in correctly classifying in certain specific
contexts or may require further fine-tuning of its hyperparameters or data preprocessing
techniques to match MLPNN’s consistency.
In terms of efficiency, MLPNN completed its execution in 27 s, while SVM took 31 s.
Although both times were relatively quick, MLPNN was not only more consistent in its
performance but also slightly more efficient in terms of execution time. These results
suggest that MLPNN may better handle certain data patterns and offer more robust and
efficient classification compared to SVM in this set of tests.
The UV-LED/RGB was shown to predict bacteria concentration in as little as half an
hour by analyzing the lag phase of the sigmoidal curve. It was previously shown that
the system quantifies bacteria concentration using the MPN method and counting how
many wells are positive at the end of the 24 h incubation period. Predicting the bacteria
concentration was performed by using trained MLPNN and SVM algorithms that predicted
which individual wells would be positive by the end of the 24 h period using only data
from the lag phase. Table 2 shows the performance of each algorithm using data from
different periods of the lag phase (3, 2, 1, and 0.5 h) and highlights the performance of
MLPNN and SVM for concentration prediction. The database was distributed accordingly:
3 h (5940 total data points: 4158 for training and 1782 for testing), 2 h (3960 data points:
2772 for training and 1188 for testing), 1 h (1980 data points: 1386 for training and 594 for
testing), and 30 min (990 data points: 693 for training and 297 for testing). The experiments
showed that it is crucial that each ML algorithm is trained with data from each lag phase
period analyzed. The prediction ultimately centers on the interaction between the signal
colors and the first derivative of each signal for the different periods of the lag phase.
While MLPNN excelled with nearly perfect metrics in sensors 0, 1, and 2 during longer
latency phases (3 h), its performance declined notably as the latency period shortened,
particularly in sensors 3, 6, and 7, where accuracy dropped as low as 0.72 at 0.5 h. This
suggests that MLPNN struggles to maintain consistency in scenarios requiring faster
response times, likely due to the complexity of the temporal data patterns. In contrast,
SVM demonstrated greater robustness across all latency phases, achieving consistently
high accuracy even in shorter latency windows. For example, while MLPNN saw a marked
reduction in performance at 0.5 h, SVM maintained relatively stable metrics, only showing
slight drops in sensors 2, 3, and 5. This resilience in SVM suggests that, although slightly
less efficient in terms of execution time, it may provide more reliable performance in real-
time or near-real-time applications where shorter latency periods are critical. Therefore,
while MLPNN offers superior classification in more stable, extended time frames, SVM
proves to be a more versatile option under dynamic temporal constraints.\n\n---\n\n## Page 97\n\nBiosensors 2025 , 15 , 284 14 of 17

 4. Conclusions
 Experiments with the UV-LED/RGB system demonstrate its strong potential for real-
time bacterial growth monitoring in water samples at the point of care. The microfluidic
device and MPN approach yielded consistent results when comparing the results to the
benchmark Quanti-Tray/2000, establishing it as a reliable, straightforward model for wa-
ter sample acquisition and monitoring. The microfluidic device was designed to have
a 166.4 CFU/100 mL detection range and for detecting and quantifying bacteria below
and above the EPA BAV value of 70 CFU/100 mL for E. faecalis , helping to reduce false
negatives. Featuring self-loading capabilities upon immersion, the microfluidic device
enables fast, user-friendly operation without requiring trained personnel. Additionally,
the UV-LED/RGB system offers portable incubation and detection, effectively maintain-
ing ideal bacterial growth conditions while monitoring bacteria growth and predicting
contamination in a short amount of time.\n\n---\n\n## Page 98\n\nBiosensors 2025 , 15 , 284 15 of 17
The system was tested using various bacterial concentrations and benchmarked
against the IDEXX Quanti-Tray/2000, demonstrating its ability to quantify bacteria growth
over a range of concentrations. The characteristic sigmoidal growth curve’s slope becomes
steeper, and the exponential phase begins earlier as the bacterial concentration increases.
Positive wells were observed even at low concentrations, confirming the system’s detection
capabilities at the EPA BAV standard for recreational water quality.
Notably, using normalized and first derivative RGBC signals as inputs in ML algo-
rithms provided a method for accelerated bacterial detection. The results show that both
the MLPNN and SVM exhibited strong classification performance, achieving a maximum
precision of 1.00 across multiple sensors for both MLPNN and SVM. Importantly, SVM
demonstrated the capability to predict the presence of bacteria in water samples within
the first 30 min of incubation, achieving perfect metrics of 1.00 for accuracy, precision,
recall, and F1 score for sensors 0, 1, and 4, with the lowest metric being 0.81 for sensor 3.
While MLPNN achieved near-perfect metrics in most cases, SVM maintained robustness
across various sensors in scenarios demanding rapid response times (30 min), deliver-
ing reliable performance using shorter lag phases, while MLPNN showed a decline in
accuracy. This comparative analysis suggests that while MLPNN excels in stable condi-
tions, SVM may be more suitable for dynamic environments requiring prompt detection.
These findings underscore the effectiveness of the UV-LED/RGB system for MPN analysis
combined with machine learning for rapid, low-cost, and portable bacteriological water
quality assessments.
The system suffers from limitations, including its detection range and resolution and
high confidence intervals (Figure 1e). Increasing the detection range and resolution and
decreasing the confidence intervals requires introducing more wells into the microfluidic
device, making it bigger, requiring more sensors, more energy for sample incubation, and
more computational power for ML analysis. This would have drawbacks, such as higher
energy requirements and reduced portability. Using only 10 mL in the microfluidic device
makes it portable but negatively affects its accuracy while making it uncertain if the sample
is representative of the environment being tested. The margins of error also increase with
sample dilution, as required when analyzing saline water. Even with these drawbacks,
the system demonstrates the ability to deliver bacteriological water quality results within
30 min in a low-cost, portable, and easy-to-use form factor, in stark contrast to traditional
laboratory-based systems, which often require specialized equipment, laboratory space,
and trained personnel.

 Conditional Diffusion Models: A Survey
of Techniques, Applications and
Challenges
THEODOR PANAGIOTAKOPOULOS 1,2 , SOTIRIS KOTSIANTIS 3 , ALEXANDROS GKILLAS 4 ,
AND ARIS S. LALOS 4 , 1 Department of Management Science and Technology, University of Patras, Patras, Greece 2 School of Business, University of Nicosia, 2417 Nicosia, Cyprus 3 Department of Mathematics, University of Patras, Patras, Greece 4 Industrial Systems Institute, Athena Research Center, Patras, Greece
Corresponding author: Theodor Panagiotakopoulos (e-mail: tpanagiotakop@upatras.gr).
This work was supported by the Horizon project CoEvolution - 101168560
 ABSTRACT Conditional diffusion models (CDMs) are an emerging family of generative models that
enable controllable, data-driven generation across a wide range of modalities. Through conditioning of
the generation process on side information such as labels, signals or physical constraints, CDMs promote
structured generation, guided sampling and stable inference in settings where complexity, uncertainty and
limited data are prevalent. This article provides a complete overview of recent advancements in CDM
architectures and, we explore their applications in several areas like computer vision, natural language
processing, mechanics, healthcare. Furthermore, we investigate the significant challenges of CDMs. We
lastly identify emerging directions and open research problems, with the goal of providing a reference paper
for researchers and practitioners engaged in the theory and application of conditional diffusion models.
 INDEX TERMS Machine learning, Conditional diffusion models, Conditional diffusion techniques,
Conditional diffusion applications

 I. INTRODUCTION
 Conditional Diffusion Models (CDMs) are an extension of
the basic paradigm of diffusion probabilistic models [1] with
external conditioning signals during generation. Similar to
vanilla diffusion models [1], CDMs learn a forward process
that successively corrupts data into noise and then learn a
reverse denoising process to regenerate structured samples.
The only difference lies in the introduction of an auxiliary
condition, which steers the generation towards target results
[2].
The diffusion lineage begins with the non-equilibrium
thermodynamics view of generative modeling [3], which set
up the forward–reverse diffusion process later made popu-
lar by DDPM/score-based models. Later milestones include
class/text-conditional denising and iterative refinement for
restoration and super-resolution (e.g., SR3) [4] and modular
conditioning mechanisms that extend text prompts with im-
age prompts through lightweight adapters (e.g., IP-Adapter)
to provide multimodal control without full fine-tuning [5].
Together, these writings sketch a path from probability-

 based diffusion into controllable, task-directed pipelines for
synthesis, editing and restoration, motivating our focus on
conditional diffusion models and their evaluation.
The conditioning input itself can take numerous forms,
such as class labels, text descriptions, semantic maps or
even partially observed data and is incorporated into the
model architecture in each denoising step. The model sees
paired data when it is trained: a clean target sample and its
corresponding condition. It predicts the denoised version of
the input, conditioned on both the noisy sample and auxiliary
signal, by learning to do this. In inference, generation starts
from a pure noise and progressively converts it into a real
sample that meets the given condition.
This conditioning enables CDMs to produce samples not
only of high quality and diversity, similar to that of uncon-
ditional diffusion models, but also controllable and semanti-
cally aligned with the target outputs. By including external
guidance into both the forward and reverse diffusion process,
CDMs overcome one of the most profound limitations of
simple diffusion models: the lack of content control over gen-
erated content. This added structure enables more targeted
usage in applications such as image-to-image translation,
text-to-image synthesis and conditioned molecule genera-
tion.
Moreover, CDMs also improve sample efficiency and gen-
eration consistency in real-world applications where some
specific outputs are required. While normal diffusion models
need to rely on post hoc filtering or sampling heuristics to
mimic target outputs, CDMs tend to guide the generative
process towards the conditions specified. This results in im-
proved alignment of the generated samples to the user intent
and reduces the computational expense of generating and
comparing various samples. In addition, conditioning also
tends to enhance training stability and convergence because
it adds an informative signal that reduces the solution space.
These advantages make CDMs a powerful framework for
bridging the gap between general-purpose generative model-
ing and application-driven content production. Since they are
modular, it is easy to integrate different conditioning mech-
anisms into them and therefore, they can easily be applied
to a variety of generative and reconstructive tasks. Stable
Diffusion, Imagen and GLIDE models are some prominent
examples of CDMs, which have shown state-of-the-art per-
formance on research as well as real-world applications.
 A. CONTRIBUTIONS
 Despite the increasing attention generated by CDMs, relevant
surveys are quite scarce and examine them through the lens
of sepecific application domains (e.g. medical imaging) or
tasks, such as text-to-image generation. A comprehensive
overview on CDNs has not yet been presented in the lit-
erature. This survey aims to address this gap, by offering
a concise and thorough examination of CDMs, bringing
together recent developments and structuring this rapidly
evolving area of research within a unified framework de-
picted in Fig. 1. While unconditional diffusion models have
already demonstrated impressive generative abilities, their
conditional counterparts take things a step further. This is
achieved by allowing for more targeted, user-guided genera-
tion tailored to specific tasks or inputs. In this work, we make
the following key contributions:
 • We present a structured exposition of the core math-
ematical foundations and architectural elements of
CDMs.
 • We propose a novel taxonomy that categorizes CDM
use cases across diverse domains, including image gen-
eration, restoration, medical imaging, remote sensing
and urban analytics. For each category, we analyze the
types of conditioning signals used and the challenges
that CDMs help address.
 • We highlight critical insights into the behavior of
CDMs, including their ability to model complex multi-
modal distributions, their robustness to noise and pertur-
bations and their effectiveness in structured generation
tasks.
 • We identify open problems and future research opportu-
nities, including improving scalability, ensuring consis-
tency across conditions, generalizing to unseen condi-
tioning signals and integrating CDMs into downstream
applications.
Conditional diffusion models (CDMs) have emerged ex-
tremely quickly from early derivations [2], [6] to production-
sparse, controllable pipelines such as latent diffusion, cas-
caded text-to-image and instruction-following editors [7]–
[11], with big syntheses charting out the space [1]. Their
application prospects vary from creative tooling and prod-
uct visualization, medical-domain imaging (restoration, seg-
mentation, artifact suppression) [12]–[15], remote sens-
ing and geospatial analysis (SR, despeckling, SAR–optical
transformation) [16]–[19], scientific discovery and simula-
tion (molecular/linker synthesis, speeded-up dynamics) [20],
[21], engineering and materials design [22]–[24], to privacy
and communications (anonymization, OFDM/semantic com-
munication) [25]–[28]. Market potential comes from the eco-
nomics of controllability—guidance and adapters send out-
puts to task constraints, reducing iteration cost [7], [10]—and
from the ability to synthesize condition-matched data in lim-
ited or regulated settings [12], [16] and slim latent pipelines
enable on-prem deployment with reproducible evaluation [7].
However, two bottlenecks require systematic investigation:
stable condition adherence under distribution shift (e.g., ex-
treme poses/layouts) [10] and the compute/latency expense
of high-resolution cascades [8]. This research addresses these
shortcomings by presenting datasets, experimental setups and
measures utilized to validate CDMs, along with guidance
toward safe, scalable and compliant deployment.
 B. HOW THIS SURVEY DIFFERS FROM PRIOR REVIEWS
 The review of diffusion models and applications that maps
out important areas of the terrain—from early methods [2],
[6] and overall syntheses [1] to image synthesis and condi-

 Dimension Representative prior work This survey
 Scope Foundations and im- age synthesis [2], [6]– [8], [29]
End-to-end view linking capability primitives to software intents
Taxonomy Task-/area-centric lists [1] Two-axis: capability prim- itives → software intents
Evidence Benchmarks-heavy [1], [7], [29] Benchmarks + field stud- ies + ops telemetry
tioning advancements [7]–[11], [29], [30]—exists, but they
cover some, not all, gaps. Table 2 summarizes the major
points of differentiation.
 a: Breadth vs. depth
 Earlier works tend to highlight either algorithmic fami-
lies and image generation [2], [6]–[8], [29] or application-
specific use (e.g., medical imaging and computational sci-
ence) [12], [13], [20], [21]. Here, we instead combine
system-level perspectives (processes, governance, adoption)
with method-level specificity (models, evaluation structure)
and provide a crosswalk from research artifact to deployable
software practice.
 b: Unifying taxonomy
 Surveys have a tendency to enumerate capabilities by task
names (generate, improve, translate) or by application do-
mains [1]. We propose a two-axis taxonomy relating ca-
pability primitives (representation, transformation, ground-
ing, control) to software intents. This resolves mismatches
where a technique is evaluated under incompatible settings
and facilitates principled comparison across modalities, like
conditioning and editing [10], [11].
 c: Evidence integration beyond benchmarks.
 Where earlier assessments target static benchmarks and visi-
ble exemplars [1], [7], [29], we triangulate benchmarks, field
studies and operations telemetry (when available) to reveal
socio-technical impacts that are not attainable by benchmarks
alone.
 d: Actionable guidance.
 Rather than concluding with general research requirements,
we boil down decision checklists, reference architectures and
migration paths that map capabilities into business objectives
and limitations, enabling teams to move from exploration
to production across modalities and domains (e.g., medical
[12], [13], molecules and dynamics [20], [21] and remote
sensing [16], [17]).
 II. MATHEMATICAL FOUNDATIONS OF CONDITIONAL
DIFFUSION MODELS
 CDMs build on the diffusion probabilistic framework by
introducing conditioning information, such as labels, class
embeddings, text prompts or other auxiliary signals, into
both the forward and reverse diffusion processes. This added
guidance allows the models to generate outputs that align
with specific inputs. CDMs are grounded in principles from
non-equilibrium thermodynamics and variational inference
[6].
 A. FORWARD DIFFUSION PROCESS
 The forward process [2] gradually perturbs a data sample x 0
 into a noise vector x T over T steps by adding Gaussian noise
at each time step. This is formally defined as a Markov chain:
 q ( x 1: T | x 0 ) =

q ( x t | x t → 1 ) = N
 (
 x t ; √ 1 → ω t x t → 1 , ω t I
 )

where ω t ↑ (0 , 1) is a variance schedule controlling the
amount of noise added at each step.
After many steps, x T becomes nearly isotropic Gaussian:
 q ( x T | x 0 ) ↓ N ( 0 , I ) .
 B. REVERSE DIFFUSION PROCESS
 The generative process [2] seeks to reverse the forward
diffusion by learning a parameterized distribution p ω ( x t → 1 |
 x t , y ) conditioned on auxiliary information y :
 p ω ( x 0: T | y ) = p ( x T )
 T ∏

 p ω ( x t → 1 | x t , y ) ,
 where typically p ( x T ) = N ( 0 , I ) .
The reverse transitions are modeled as Gaussian distribu-
tions with learned means:
 p ω ( x t → 1 | x t , y ) = N ( x t → 1 ; μ ω ( x t , t, y ) , ε 2 t I ) .
 C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
 Training is done by minimizing a variational bound on the
negative log-likelihood: log p ω ( x 0 | y ) . This leads to a sim-
plified loss function derived from denoising score matching:
 L simple ( ϑ ) = E x 0 , ω ,t

 D. CONDITIONING MECHANISMS
 Conditional information [29] y can be incorporated into the
denoising network ω ω ( · ) using various techniques:
 • Directly concatenating y to the input features or latent
representation.
 • Applying attention mechanisms to align x t and y , com-
monly used in text-to-image diffusion models.
 • Adaptive normalization: Modifying the normalization
layers (e.g., AdaGN, AdaIN) in the network using y as
a conditioning vector.

 E. SAMPLING
 At inference time, sampling starts from Gaussian noise x T ↘
 N (0 , I ) and proceeds iteratively using the learned reverse
process:
 x t → 1 ↘ p ω ( x t → 1 | x t , y ) , for t = T, T → 1 , . . . , 1 .
 The final output x 0 is a sample from the conditional distribu-
tion p ω ( x 0 | y ) .
 F. INTERPRETATION AND APPLICATIONS
 From a probabilistic standpoint, CDMs approximate the con-
ditional distribution p ( x 0 | y ) through a sequence of denois-
ing transformations. Their ability to flexibly incorporate side
information makes them suitable for a wide range of tasks,
such as:
 • Class-conditional image generation
 • Text-to-image synthesis
 • Image-to-image translation
 • Adversarial defense and privacy-preserving synthesis
 This mathematical framework (see Algorithm 1) forms
the backbone of conditional diffusion modeling, enabling
diverse applications while offering strong generative fidelity
and controllability.
 G. DATASETS, EXPERIMENTAL SETUPS AND METRICS
FOR VALIDATING CONDITIONAL DIFFUSION MODELS
 Benchmarking datasets are required to measure the perfor-
mance and generalization of CDMs across a broad variety
of tasks. They provide standardized inputs and ground truth

 outputs that allow researchers to compare models in a repro-
ducible and fair manner. For image-to-image translation and
enhancement tasks, benchmark datasets are DIV2K, CelebA-
HQ and FFHQ. DIV2K is a popular dataset for super-
resolution and denoising and it contains high-resolution natu-
ral images that permit downsampling-based testing. CelebA-
HQ and FFHQ are face datasets of high quality that are

 used for tasks like face synthesis, inpainting and privacy-
preserving generation, in which identity, expression and at-
tribute conditioning are required.
For text-to-image generation, the benchmark datasets typ-
ically used are MS-COCO, CUB-200 and LAION. MS-
COCO provides densely annotated everyday scenes with
diverse captions, enabling evaluation of a model’s capac-
ity to generate conditionally consistent images with tex-
tual prompts. CUB-200 is a fine-grained bird dataset used
for more specialized studies where accuracy in capturing
subtle visual differences (e.g., species-specific attributes) is
tested. LAION, especially its larger versions (e.g., LAION-
400M, LAION-5B), provides large-scale text-image pairs
web-crawled, hence suitable for training and testing mod-
els on general, diverse and commonly noisy text prompts.
These datasets are responsible for measuring not just realism,
but also semantic alignment and diversity of the outputs.
In domain-specific applications like medical imaging and
remote sensing, CDMs are evaluated on task-specific datasets
like BraTS (brain tumor MRI scans), LIDC-IDRI (lung CT
data) and SEN12MS (multispectral satellite images).
The datasets described above and summarized in Table
3, allow for benchmarking models on tasks like modal-
ity translation, anomaly detection, super-resolution and
segmentation-guided generation. It is important to use such
domain-specific benchmarks to ensure that CDMs are not
just generically powerful but also reliable, safe and precise in
high-stakes applications. Furthermore, benchmarking on di-
verse datasets enables probing robustness, bias and fairness,
so that CDMs can be responsibly applied across a variety
of applications. In Table 4, one can see typical datasets by
domain.
Table 5 summarizes quantitative and qualitative metrics
used to assess CDMs across tasks and domains. Fréchet
Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) are widely
used to gauge realism and diversity in diffusion-based image
synthesis [7], [8], [29]. FID measures the statistical prox-
imity between real and generated image distributions, while
IS reflects how confidently a pretrained classifier annotates
generated images and the heterogeneity of predicted labels
[7], [29]. For text-conditional settings, the CLIP Score has
become a robust indicator of semantic correspondence be-
tween prompts and outputs, particularly in modern text-to-
image pipelines [8], [30].
Other than image quality and semantic correspondence,
other metrics capture structural fidelity and task-specific
accuracy. PSNR and SSIM are especially effective for low-
level vision applications like super-resolution or denois-
ing—capturing reconstruction fidelity and perceptual sim-
ilarity between the reference and synthesized images [7],
[13], [16], [17]. For image editing applications, edit accuracy
or success-rate metrics help measure how closely a model
adheres to text-based instructions [8], [11]. Furthermore,
computational scores including inference time and training
efficiency are increasingly decisive for real-world feasibility,
with latent pipelines explicitly trading small quality drops

 For reproducibility and for simple comparison, one should

 • Splits and filtering: train/val/test protocol; class/caption

tween train and test).

 III. PROMINENT CONDITIONAL DIFFUSION MODELS
 In recent years, CDMs have become a powerful approach
to generative modeling, capable of producing high-quality
results guided by external inputs. A number of standout
models have shaped and extended the potential of CDMs,
especially in the realm of image generation. In this section,
we spotlight some of the most influential models and out-
line their defining features. Based on this analysis, Table 6
presents a comparative overview, while Table 7 summarizes
the main advantages and limitations of each model and Table
8 provide a visual trade-off analysis.
 A. STABLE DIFFUSION
 Stable Diffusion [7] is one of the most widely used latent
diffusion models (LDMs), known for performing denoising
in a compressed latent space rather than directly in pixel
space—making it much more computationally efficient. It
uses a text encoder, such as CLIP or T5, to extract mean-
ingful representations from textual prompts, which are then
incorporated into the denoising process via cross-attention
mechanisms. To strike a balance between conditional and
unconditional generation, Stable Diffusion applies classifier-
free guidance, enhancing both image quality and prompt
alignment. Its open-source nature and flexibility have made it
a foundational model in the field of text-to-image generation.
 B. IMAGEN
 Developed by Google Research, Imagen [8] combines the
strengths of large pretrained language models, like T5, for
text encoding with a cascaded diffusion framework. It gener-
ates images in stages, starting from a low-resolution version
and gradually refining them to higher resolutions, with each
step guided by the input text. Imagen stands out for its
state-of-the-art performance on multiple image generation
benchmarks, highlighting how crucial strong language rep-
resentations are for effective conditioning.
 C. DALLE-2
 Although not a traditional diffusion model, DALLE-2 [30]
from OpenAI incorporates diffusion techniques as part of its
two-stage image generation process. In the first stage, it trans-
lates text prompts into image embeddings using a CLIP-like
model. The second stage then uses a diffusion model (or a
similar approach) to produce high-quality images that match
these embeddings. DALLE-2’s ability to generate diverse,
visually rich content from complex textual descriptions has
made it one of the most influential systems in the generative
AI landscape.

 D. GLIDE
 GLIDE (Guided Language-to-Image Diffusion for Genera-
tion and Editing) citeNichol2022 is also one of the renowned
CDMs that supports unconditional and conditional image
generation. It employs classifier-free guidance and accepts
text prompts or low-resolution images as conditions. GLIDE
was the initial diffusion-based model to support image edit-
ing based on reversibility of diffusion and conditional con-
trol.
 E. CONTROLNET
 ControlNet [10] is an add-on to recent diffusion models such
as Stable Diffusion wherein there is fine-grained control of
the generation process with structured inputs such as edge
maps, depth maps or human poses. It introduces extra control
pathways to the default U-Net architecture and employs joint
training so as to preserve the model’s capacity for following
both natural language and low-level visual instructions. Con-
trolNet has enabled new task-specific generation and editing.
 F. INSTRUCTPIX2PIX
 InstructPix2Pix [11] takes image editing one step further by
conditioning the diffusion model on both the input image
and a natural language instruction. It fine-tunes a pre-trained
text-to-image diffusion model to carry out edits like "make
it a sunny day" or "convert it to a sketch," enabling intuitive,
instruction-based visual manipulation.
 IV. MEDICINE AND BIOMEDICINE
 CDMs have emerged as powerful tools across medical and
biomedical applications, ushering in immense advancement
in image synthesis, signal enhancement and data-driven dis-
covery. By conditioning on structured inputs ranging from
imaging modalities (CT, MRI, X-ray) to anatomical anno-
tations and diagnostic labels, these models can generate ex-
tremely realistic outputs that are indistinguishable from real-
world data. Their abilities go beyond generation, providing
advantages in applications like super-resolution, denoising,
modality translation and artifact removal, thereby solving
fundamental challenges in clinical workflow and medical
research.
One of the most important benefits of CDMs is that they
can generate diverse and realistic medical images conditional
on disease pathology. A model, for instance, can be trained
on X-rays of the chest to create synthetic images for disease
labels like pneumonia or COVID-19. The images enhance
training sets, generalize better and decrease the need for
expensive, manually annotated medical data, which is not just
ethically tenuous but also resource-expensive to procure.
In image-to-image translation applications, CDMs have
been successful in improving low-quality scans (e.g., via
super-resolution), modality translation (e.g., CT to MRI) and
retaining fine anatomical details. This kind of functionality is
particularly useful in low-resource environments or settings
with restricted imaging hardware. In addition, by producing
"healthy" baseline counterparts for comparison, CDMs are
capable of facilitating anomaly detection by emphasizing
pathology-related deviations.
The recent development of denoising diffusion probabilis-
tic models achieved success in image synthesis tasks. Al-
though some works attempted to investigate the capability of
the models in image semantic segmentation, their application
was restricted in Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation
(WSSS). The research [12] illustrated the application of
category-aware semantic information in CDMs for object
mask prediction using image-level annotations alone. By
approximating the derivative of CDM output, the target class
would be able to be predicted independently without exter-
nal classifiers, which may bring noise. The novel approach
surpassed existing methods on medical image segmentation
datasets and was more efficient, with the potential to be
applied elsewhere. Recent studies demonstrate the breadth
of CDM applications in medical domains, as summarized in
Table 9.
 A. BIOMEDICAL SIGNAL PROCESSING AND DRUG
DISCOVERY
 CDMs were also promising in signal processing and phar-
maceutical simulation. In neurophysiology, [34] presented
EEGDfus, a dual-branch CNN–Transformer model that
achieved state-of-the-art EEG signal denoising performance.
The model achieved new records on public data sets, demon-
strating that CDMs can effectively process temporal and
spatial complexities in biomedical signals.
For drug discovery, [35] proposed DiffFBDD, a protein-
pocket-driven CDM utilizing geometric and atomic condi-
tioning with equivariant graph neural networks. The model
produced ligand fragments with favorable binding and re-
duced computation time. Building on this path, [20] proposed
DiffLinker, a 3D CDM for designing synthetically tractable
molecular linkers, which surpassed traditional approaches to
fragment-based drug design.
 1) Clinical and Diagnostic Imaging Equipment
 CDMs played a big role in diagnostic precision. Wu et al.
[13] proposed MaC-DM to generate pediatric fracture X-
rays for training stronger classifiers, particularly for CML
fractures, which comprises a key marker in non-accidental
injury evaluation. In dermatology, Benjdira et al. [36] pro-
posed DM-AHR, a self-supervised method that eliminated
hair artifacts from dermoscopic images based on a care-
fully curated dataset (DERMAHAIR), improving lesions’
visibility. Xu et al. [31] addressed image fusion by merging
CT, MRI and PET inputs in TFS-Diff, which was strength-
ened with uncertainty-aware channel attention for generating
diagnostically enhanced fused images. In gastroenterology,
Du et al. [14] proposed PolypSegDiff, a multi-scale CDM,
that reached state-of-the-art results in segmenting concealed
polyps from endoscopic videos.

 TABLE 7. Advantages and Disadvantages of Prominent Conditional Diffusion Models
 Model Advantages Disadvantages (with concrete examples) Stable Diffusion [7] - Efficient generation via compressed latent space (faster sampling, lower VRAM) - Open-source ecosystem (LoRA, Control- Net, adapters) - Classifier-free guidance enables controlla- bility
- Latent compression can drop micro-details (e.g., small text on signage, fine fabric textures) - Prompt/CFG sensitivity; high guidance can cause saturation or washed colors (e.g., CFG ↑ 12) - Layout drift and limb artifacts in complex scenes (hands/fingers, occlusions) - Quality varies across community checkpoints; safety/bias depends on trained data Imagen [8] - State-of-the-art photorealism in cascade (64 ↓ 256 ↓ 1024) - Strong text understanding via T5 condition- ing - Cascaded SR improves local detail
- Not open-source; model/dataset access restricted - High compute cost from multi-stage pipeline (slow wall-clock for 1024px) - Still struggles with rare proper nouns and exact spelling in-text renders
DALLE-2 [30] - Diverse, compositionally rich outputs with CLIP-guided prior - Strong zero-shot prompt following - Good at concept blending and styles
- Limited customization (API access; weights not released) - Spatial relations and counting can fail (e.g., “three red cubes left of two blue spheres”) - Text rendering and hands remain brittle in photorealistic scenes GLIDE [9] - Supports both text-to-image and image editing (inpainting) - Classifier-free guidance - Accepts text or image conditions
- Lower fidelity vs. later latent models (e.g., SD/Imagen) - Released weights are smaller/filtered; less diverse training set - Edit locality can bleed into untouched regions without careful masks
ControlNet [10] - Fine-grained control from structured inputs (Canny, depth, pose, seg.) - Drop-in adapters for many base models - Joint language + visual conditioning possi- ble
- Requires accurate condition maps; noisy Canny/depth induces artifacts (e.g., broken limbs, jagged edges) - Extra VRAM/latency for multiple control branches; training adapters adds complexity - Generalization degrades for out-of-distribution conditions (extreme poses/layouts) InstructPix2Pix [11] - Natural language-based image editing aligned with human instructions - Intuitive, interactive manipulation - Good for localized semantic/style edits
- Limited to editing existing images; no pure T2I - Abstract/multi-step instructions may fail or overgeneralize (e.g., “make it nostalgic but futuristic”) - Can over-edit non-target regions without masks; global relighting may intro- duce halos/banding
 B. MRI SYNTHESIS AND BRAIN IMAGING
 MRI synthesis has been an interest for CDM tasks. Dor-
jsembe et al. [37] proposed Med-DDPM, a 3D semantic
diffusion model, synthesizing anatomically valid brain MRIs
and enhancing tumor segmentation performance when ap-
plied in combination with real data. Mao et al. [38] proposed
DisC-Diff, disentangling contrast features of various MRI
types, realizing efficient super-resolution with uncertainty
estimation. In the case of neurodegenerative disease research
with limited data, Yao et al. [39] fused Alzheimer’s and
MCI patient brain scans, drastically enhancing classification
results. Wilms et al. [40] also illustrated the viability of
small-footprint wavelet-based CDMs for accurate brain age
prediction even on consumer-level hardware, while providing
interpretable counterfactual imaging. Paper [47] addressed
the challenge to reconstruct high-quality images with accu-
rate semantics from brain recordings since representations of
brain signals are intricate and there are no data annotations
available. The research proposed MinD-Vis, which learned
self-supervised representations of fMRI data through mask
modeling and a double-conditioned latent diffusion model.
Results demonstrated that MinD-Vis was able to reconstruct
images of comparable details from brain recordings with lim-
ited paired annotations, surpassing state-of-the-art techniques
in semantic mapping and generation quality. The article
provided qualitative and quantitative comparisons, demon-
strating considerable improvement in semantic classification
and image generation quality.

 C. COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY AND RELATED
MODALITIES
 In CT imaging, CDMs have excelled in tasks ranging from
reconstruction, denoising, super-resolution and artifact re-
moval. Liu et al. [41] proposed a CDM-based approach to
reconstruct high-fidelity CT images from just two views
with Noise-Adaptive Total Variation (NATV) regularization
for better fidelity, which is of practical use in industrial
inspections. Shi et al. [42], [48] applied CDMs in Electrical
Impedance Tomography (EIT) with transformer-based mod-
els (CDEIT, CDMVC) that generalised and reconstructed
better.
Ye et al. [43] presented a CDM to investigate the strength-
ening of trabecular bone texture in femur CTs, achieving
ultra-high-resolution images necessary for bone microarchi-
tecture analysis. In another line of research, Luo et al. [15]
presented BCDMAR, which addressed metal artifacts in CT
images through bi-constraint conditioning, preserving the
structure of tissues near metallic implants. Gao et al. [44]
presented CoCoDiff, which performed slice-wise denoising
in low-dose CT by reversing noise accumulation tendencies
through contextual guidance.
 D. BIOLOGICAL APPLICATIONS
 The paper [49] proposed DiffusionPix2Pix, a diffusion-based
improved model for synthetic image generation. Previous
images were leveraged in the model to achieve better per-
formance than current state-of-the-art models, i.e., Pix2Pix-
G and Pix2Pix-GD, on sample diversity, fidelity and Fréchet
Inception Distance. DiffusionPix2Pix enabled regression-
conditional image-to-image translation with a binary mask
and achieved superior performance in a plant disease dataset
generation with accurate disease degree control. Experimen-
tal findings revealed that the model had better precision,

was thus appropriate for application in tasks that called for

The paper [50] proposed a new framework named Diffu-
sionAAE for hyperspectral image classification to combat
high dimensionality and few labeled data. DiffusionAAE
integrated Adversarial Autoencoders with conditional dif-
fusion models, which infused spectral similarity constraints
and class label guidance for synthesizing realistic samples.
The model was two-staged: an AAE learned spectral-spatial
relations and a diffusion model added features with physical
constraints preserved. Experiments on benchmark datasets
demonstrated that DiffusionAAE performed better than state-
of-the-art methods and attained high accuracies in Indian
Pines, University of Pavia and Salinas datasets. Specifically,
it performed extremely well in classifying minority classes
and performed well with limited training data and was an
efficient tool for ecological monitoring applications.
 V. SATELLITE IMAGERY
 CDMs have emerged as groundbreaking techniques within
the context of satellite imagery, offering a broad array of
functionality ranging from image creation, image enhance-
ment, to semantic interpretation. The advantages of such
models include the ability to condition on varied contextual
inputs such as geospatial coordinates, land-use types, sea-
sonal cycles or historical imagery, thus creating temporally
coherent and visually realistic satellite views. This flexibil-
ity is particularly valuable for use in applications such as
environmental monitoring and disaster response, for which
prompt and high-resolution access to data frequently is lim-
ited by cloud cover or revisit period for satellites.
In addition to image synthesis, CDMs increasingly are
applied to enhancement operations such as super-resolution,
cloud removal and image fusion. Through noisy or occluded
observation conditioning, such models have the ability to
synthesize high-fidelity outputs with critical spatial informa-
tion, such as infrastructure, foliage or water bodies, thus in-
creasing the operational utility and interpretability of satellite
imagery. Moreover, the generative nature of CDMs enables
synthetic imagery generation to accommodate tailored land-
use or developmental contexts. This aspect is vital to train
downstream machine learning models, especially in under-
represented or data-scarce regions.
In general, CDMs significantly enhance the use of satel-
lite image analysis by completing gaps in data, improving
image resolution and enabling predictive visualizations in
a wide range of geospatial and temporal applications. The
applications of CDMs in satellite and remote sensing imagery
is discussed in the following sections and a summary is
provided in Table 10.
 A. REMOTE SENSING APPLICATIONS
 CDMs have been embraced in remote sensing for applica-
tions that are varied in nature, including super-resolution,
spatiotemporal fusion, classification and data augmentation.
Their capacity to work with advanced image priors and noise
renders them apt for real-world applications where sensor
capability and sparsity of data are common.
For instance, Ref-Diff [51] addresses problems of
reference-based super-resolution (RefSR), specifically chal-
lenging texture detail transfer at high scaling factors. By
employing land cover change priors, the model is able to im-
prove denoising and texture reconstruction in both dynamic
and static regions and outperforms existing RefSR algorithms
in terms of resolution and accuracy.
Based on multi-source fusion, Ma et al. [52] built a CDM-
based model, where Gaussian noise was used to model cross-
sensor discrepancies. Their encoder-decoder network effec-
tively combined imagery between sensors and time while
maintaining spatial coherence even under altering environ-
mental conditions.
Han et al. [16] proposed EHC-DMSR, a hybrid archi-
tecture of CNNs and Transformers with a high-frequency
Fourier-domain constraint. The computationally efficient
model utilizes a feature distillation approach to produce
sharp, high-resolution outputs with enhanced boundary defi-
nition.
Along with reducing inference latency, FastDiffSR [17]
was proposed as a light-weight alternative that also features
channel and spatial attention modules. It minimizes sampling
steps in the diffusion process without compromising percep-
tual fidelity, with competitive performance on a number of
measures.
In categorization, MCDiff [53] is focused on PolSAR
imagery, blending previous knowledge with noise modeling
and spectro-spatial high-order statistical feature extraction. It
addresses issues such as label ambiguity and speckle noise
and performs higher accuracy and robustness on various
benchmarks.
For surface water estimation, DiffWater [54] utilizes a
CDM model tailored for noisy CYGNSS data. The model
integrates domain-specific denoising methods for improving
surface water fraction (SWF) estimation with RMSE and
correlation score improvements.
Extending CDMs to 3D sensing, SFADiff [56] addresses
autofocusing problems for millimeter-wave radar. Through
approximating 3D focused images from single-frequency
defocused inputs, the model enables high-accuracy imaging
for security and industrial applications.
The work [57] proposed a novel approach to infrared
small-target detection in computer vision using a deep gen-
erative model. ISTD-diff model progressively synthesized
a target mask from the noisy input. It had a two-pathway
architecture consisting of a conditional prior stream and a
denoising stream, both using novel channel-dimension trans-
former layers to extract the global correlations in an efficient
manner. Additionally, an attention injection module was pro-
posed to boost the denoising stream. Experimental outcomes
proved that ISTD-diff worked better than current state-of-the-
art segmentation-based approaches on small-target detection.

The spatial and spectral fidelity is enhanced, blurring is
resistant and the approach outperforms other algorithms.
Overall, these efforts emphasize the versatility of CDMs
in remote sensing and deliver robust, data-sparse solutions to
numerous enhancement and interpretation tasks.
 B. ASTROPHYSICAL IMAGERY
 CDMs also hold great promise for the enhancement of astro-
nomical images, particularly in situations where resolution
is constrained by telescope hardware or atmospheric turbu-
lence.
DiffLense [32] employs CDMs to enhance images of
gravitational lensing captured with the Hyper Suprime-Cam
(HSC) using high-quality Hubble Space Telescope (HST) im-
ages as conditional input. The method enables the restoration
of fine details with background noise suppression, outper-
forming traditional super-resolution approaches.
In a different line of investigation, Doorenbos et al. [55]
developed a generative AI model that predicts optical galaxy
spectra from multiband photometric images. The approach
combines diffusion modeling and contrastive learning, allow-
ing for the extraction of galaxy properties (e.g., metallicity,
velocity dispersion, photometric redshift) in the absence of
spectroscopy. The approach was validated with Sloan Dig-
ital Sky Survey data and proved to be highly valuable for
automating large-scale surveys and mock catalog generation.
These activities illustrate the value of CDMs for aug-
menting the analytical capability of astrophysical images,
particularly where direct measurement is excessively costly
or impossible.
 C. SYNTHETIC APERTURE RADAR (SAR) IMAGING
 SAR imaging offers critical advantages in Earth observation
via its weather- and light-independent sensing. However, its
interpretability is consistently undermined by speckle noise
and low visual acuity, a superior area for CDM-based en-
hancement.
SFDiff [18] addresses the SAR-to-optical translation task
by introducing a model with spatial-frequency refinement
mechanisms, including a context prior extractor and com-
plementary learning modules. The suggested architecture
maintains structural consistency and details in the translated
images, which enables applications like cross-modal object
detection.
In despeckling, DiffusionSAR [19] employs a novel ap-
proach of gamma noise modeling and domain-specific trans-
formations (e.g., Yeo-Johnson) for speckle removal with
fine structure preservation. The model obtains state-of-the-
art results on both synthetic and real-world SAR data, where
multitemporal fine-tuning is crucial for domain adaptation.
By improving SAR image fidelity and interpretability,
these CDM-based methods significantly increase the utility
of radar-based Earth observation for agriculture, defense and
disaster management applications.
