 VI. INVERSE MULTI-DIMENSIONAL PROBLEMS
 A. SUPER-RESOLUTION
 Super-resolution is the ill-posed problem of interpolating a
low-resolution (LR) image to a high-resolution (HR) version
in order to recreate fine structures, textures and structural
detail. As an ill-posed problem in itself, where multiple
potential HR images can be the result of one LR input, tradi-
tional approaches such as interpolation or sparse coding cre-
ate excessively smoothed or blurred output. Recent advances
in deep learning, particularly with the use of convolutional
neural networks (CNNs) and generative adversarial networks
 VOLUME 4, 2016 11
 This article has been accepted for publication in IEEE Access. This is the author's version which has not been fully edited and content may change prior to final publication. Citation information: DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3625094
 This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License. For more information, see https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/\n\n---\n\n## Page 112\n\nAuthor et al. : Preparation of Papers for IEEE TRANSACTIONS and JOURNALS
 (GANs), have significantly improved the visual and quantita-
tive fidelity of reconstructed images. However, these methods
typically face challenges in producing photorealistic textures
for ambiguous regions and tend to form visual artifacts or
unrealistic hallucinations.
CDMs offer a promising alternative in the form of a re-
design of super-resolution as conditional generative process.
Here, the model is trained to denoise a high-resolution image
from noise, conditioned on the LR observation. Unlike deter-
ministic approaches, diffusion models sample from a learned
distribution, allowing for multiple potential HR outputs. This
is an advantage reflecting the inherent uncertainty in im-
puting missing high-frequency information. This stochastic
sampling is particularly useful in capturing fine textures such
as foliage, clothes patterns or hairs that are typically lost
in LR observations. Besides, CDMs are hallucination- and
visual artifact-resilient compared to GANs and can be guided
by perceptual, semantic or structural priors for enhancing
realism and fidelity.
Experiments have now shown the effectiveness of CDMs
in addressing a wide variety of super-resolution applications.
Rouhiainen et al. [59], for example, applied the Palette model
to volumetric data to increase cosmological simulations’
resolution by 8 ! without degrading key statistical metrics.
The work illustrates the versatility of diffusion models in sci-
entific computing where physical realism is the top priority.
On another note, Niu et al. [60] responded to the com-
putational inefficiencies of classical diffusion models with
ACDMSR, a method that replaces deterministic denoising
with stochastic sampling. This approach significantly reduces
inference time without compromising on competitive per-
formance on benchmark data, proving the realizability of
diffusion models for real-time or low-resource settings.
In addition to both fidelity and speed, Wang et al. [45]
introduced a super-resolution model based on mean-reverting
stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with the addition
of new components like ENAFBlocks, adaptive sampling
and LR encoding. These architectural improvements pro-
vided state-of-the-art performance across a range of datasets,
demonstrating that diffusion models can be optimized in a
systematic way.
CDMs have also been advantageous to specialized do-
mains. Chen et al. [61] proposed BISRM to enhance borehole
images used in geotechnical exploration. Through the blend-
ing of multi-region attention with a conditional diffusion,
the model significantly improved image sharpness and detail,
which is crucial in interpreting subsurface structure.
The flexibility of CDMs extends to more challenging set-
tings such as HDR super-resolution. Yan et al. [62] addressed
the ghosting and color artifacts problem in LDR to HDR
conversion through a feature-conditioned diffusion model.
Their approach was able to remove distortions caused by
motion and achieve improved visual quality, showing the
adaptability of CDMs to dynamic scenes and high dynamic
range.
The work [63] introduced a new method, Self-Supervised
Reference-based Image Super-Resolution (SSR-SR), to gen-
erate reference images automatically for super-resolution
tasks without manual picking. The SSR-SR method used
a conditional diffusion model and self-supervised learning
to synthesize reference images closely corresponding to the
input image in semantics. These reference images were then
enhanced using a diffusion-based super-resolution model,
with additional modules ensuring proper texture transfer
and alignment. Experimental results showed that SSR-SR
achieved competitive performance on certain benchmarks
without the requirement of paired data, showing the strength
of diffusion models and self-supervised learning in advanc-
ing image super-resolution techniques.
The work [33] presented a conditional diffusion model for
point cloud upsampling, which treats a sparse input point
cloud as the condition and generates a dense point cloud.
PUDM directly learns to map noise to a high-density point
cloud, conditioned on the sparse input, rather than relying
on separate upsampling modules. A dual mapping strategy is
used to better utilize point-wise features: the model learns
the gradient of the data distribution of dense points while
being guided by the sparse set. PUDM showed strong noise-
robustness and achieved state-of-the-art results on standard
upsampling benchmarks PU-1K and PU-GAN (significantly
lower Chamfer and Hausdorff distances than previous meth-
ods).
The work [53] introduced an advancement over PUDM fo-
cusing on noisy input point clouds. PDANS (Point Diffusion
with Adaptive Noise Suppression) adds an Adaptive Noise
Suppression module to the conditional diffusion pipeline.
This module assigns weights to points based on a neigh-
borhood analysis, effectively down-weighting or removing
outlier points before and during diffusion sampling, so that
noise and outliers in the input don’t propagate into the
output. Additionally, a Tree-Transformer (TreeTrans) block
is introduced to capture correlations between high-level and
low-level features for better feature conditioning.
The work [64] proposed a fast and high-fidelity upsam-
pling approach for LiDAR point clouds based on condi-
tional diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs). Their method
conditions the diffusion process using inpainting masks,
allowing the model to generate dense point clouds from
sparse LiDAR scans. The pipeline achieves 4 ! upsampling
on KITTI-360 and demonstrates strong generalization across
datasets, while offering significantly faster inference (up to
39 ! ) compared to previous diffusion-based methods.
Taken together, these developments underscore the
promise of conditional diffusion models to transform super-
resolution. With their capacity to generate diverse, high-
fidelity outputs—even on under-constrained or ambiguous
inputs—these models are a compelling replacement for tra-
ditional deep learning models, with far-reaching uses from
astrophysics and geology to natural image denoising.

 B. LOW-LIGHT IMAGE ENHANCEMENT
 Low-light image improvement aims to boost the visibility,
contrast and perception quality of images captured in low-
light situations, i.e., nighttime or dimly lit interiors. Images
from such situations are degraded by various factors, such
as high noise, low contrast, color distortion and loss of
minute details. Traditional techniques, as well as some recent
state-of-the-art deep learning techniques, usually handle all
these collectively, generally producing artifacts or sacrificing
perceptual realism.
Conditional diffusion models offer a principled approach
to low-light enhancement via learning an iterative denoising
process conditioned on the degraded input. CDMs don’t
globally transform or handcraft filtering but learn to recon-
struct clean, well-lit images as a series of noise-removal
operations that can iteratively improve the texture and color
accuracy. Their generative nature allows for subtle recon-
struction, which makes them particularly valuable in restor-
ing fine details without noise and distortion.
One of the advantages of CDMs is that they are versa-
tile: they can be tailored to incorporate auxiliary data like
semantic tags, physics priors or metadata to guide the process
of improvement. This enables them to be domain-agnostic
across areas, from consumer photography and medical imag-
ing to surveillance and autonomous systems. Additionally,
their robust generation pipeline enables them to generate
aesthetically appealing results which remain functionally rel-
evant for subsequent processes like object detection or scene
understanding.
Among the latest publications, Wan et al. [65] introduced
the Patch-based Simplified Conditional Diffusion Model
(PSC Diffusion) that integrates light-weight U-Net architec-
ture and SimpleGate and SimPF attention blocks. Effortfully
optimized, the model enjoys patch-based training and global
regularization for simplicity preservation in high perceptual
quality. Experimental evaluations confirmed that PSC Dif-
fusion significantly outperforms baseline models, with over
35% speedup sampling speed and improved visual clarity.
Similarly, Kang et al. [66] introduced a Retinex-inspired
diffusive model that decomposes images into reflectance
and illumination components. With physically interpretable
features as directions to denoise, the model retains brightness
and structure in the dark regions. Its fusion-based condition-
ing enables proper combination of intrinsic image factors,
achieving improved restoration and more realistic-looking
outcomes.
They highlight the promise of CDMs as state-of-the-
art low-light augmentation technologies. By bridging data-
driven learning and constraint-guided physical modeling,
they offer a compelling compromise of flexibility, efficiency
and image quality—supporting more resilient vision systems
in low-illumination conditions.
A summary of the works that applied CDMs for super-
resolution and low-light image enhancement is provided in
Table 11.
 C. IMAGE RESTORATION
 Image restoration is a fundamental problem in computer vi-
sion that aims to recover an original clean high-quality image
from a degraded or corrupted version. The degradations can
result from noise, motion blur, compression artifacts, lost
data such as pixels or outside damage such as occlusions or
scratches. Traditional methods generally utilize handcrafted
priors and deterministic models, which fail to generalize and
most often produce overly smoothed or visually inconsistent
outcomes.
On the other hand, conditional diffusion models offer a
powerful generative model for restoration. Learned to reverse
a degradation process by denoising an image in sequence,
conditioned on the degraded input, these models are versatile
and capable of generating realistic textures, restoring fine
details and inpainting missing content without sacrificing
the semantic coherence of the original scene. Irrespective of
whether denoising, deblurring or inpainting is the problem in
question, conditional diffusion models can generate not just
accurate but also diverse plausible reconstructions, which is a
highly important feature when there is uncertainty or absent
data. Their robustness and versatility make them especially
worthwhile in harsh conditions such as underwater imaging,
adverse weather, low-light settings or signal-degraded im-
ages.
Li et al. [67] explored this feasibility in the context of
underwater hyperspectral image restoration and target detec-
tion, proposing a joint framework based on spectral group
extraction coupled with image enhancement and detection.
A conditional diffusion model was leveraged to generate
different spectral image groups, improving restoration per-
formance as well as target recognition efficacy. Their Joint
Underwater Hyperspectral Restoration and Detection (JU-
RTD) framework achieved better results compared to existing
methods based on better performance on synthetic and real-
world datasets. Si et al. [68] introduced CASSIDiff , the first
diffusion-based approach to hyperspectral cube reconstruc-
tion in Coded Aperture Snapshot Spectral Imaging (CASSI)
systems. The model also prioritized perceptual quality with
LPIPS and FID scores over traditional MSE and PSNR. The
model combined wavelet-based feature fusion and spatial-
spectral attention with the aim of enhancing consistency and
denoising. Experimental results on synthetic and real data
sets demonstrated its excellence.
Similarly, Yue et al. [69] addressed image degradation
under harsh weather conditions where any or all of the
degradation types (e.g., haze, rain, blur) may occur at the
same time. Their solution was the Joint Conditional Diffusion
Model (JCDM), which consists of a physical degradation
model, a degradation mask and a refinement network. This
arrangement enabled the model to restore color and texture
more precisely through the utilization of learned priors as
well as the imposition of explicit physical constraints. Com-
prehensive experiments also confirmed that JCDM consis-
tently surpassed state-of-the-art restoration methods under
complex environmental conditions.

In yet another usage context, Kim et al. [27] demonstrated
the effectiveness of conditional diffusion for image recovery
from noisy wireless transmission, specifically in orthogo-
nal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) systems. Their
framework used modulation-aware conditioning and vari-
ance learning to rectify noise-induced distortion as well as
higher-order modulation. Experiments showed significantly
enhanced PSNR(up to 8 dB for low-SNR settings) highlight-
ing the potential of conditional diffusion models in rectifying
artifacts due to transmission in real-world communication
systems.
Apart from natural imaging, conditional diffusion models
have also shown promise in particular biomedical imaging
tasks. Liu et al. [70] proposed PU-CDM, a pyramid UNet-
hierarchical conditional diffusion model specifically tailored
for sparse-view reconstruction of electron paramagnetic res-
onance imaging (EPRI). Integrating pyramid pooling, dense
connections, self-attention and predicting the noise, PU-
CDM achieved artifact suppression and structural detail by
only five denoising iterations. This made it non-applicable for
fast scanning scenarios and hinted towards potential applica-
tions in MRI, low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) and
overall image processing operations that require high-quality
reconstruction from sparse data.
The study [71] introduced a new technique called Cycle-
Conditional Diffusion Model (Cycle-CDM) to improve qual-
ity and reliability of diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) using
noise correction. Cycle-CDM utilized unpaired data learning
in order to minimize the disparity between noisy and noise-
free DWIs, generating high-quality images without paired
datasets. By introducing synthesized anatomical priors and
constraints to preserve anatomical consistency, Cycle-CDM
learned noise distribution well and generated accurate de-
noising. Simulation and clinical data experiments confirmed
that Cycle-CDM outperformed other methods in noise cor-
rection with data even from different MRI scanners. De-
noised DWI data produced by Cycle-CDM properly pre-
served tissue microstructure, which enhanced their medical
utility.
Finally, Si et al. [68] introduced CASSIDiff , the first
diffusion-based approach to hyperspectral cube reconstruc-
tion in Coded Aperture Snapshot Spectral Imaging (CASSI)
systems. The model also prioritized perceptual quality with
LPIPS and FID scores over traditional MSE and PSNR. The
model combined wavelet-based feature fusion and spatial-
spectral attention with the aim of enhancing consistency and
denoising. Experimental results on synthetic and real data
sets demonstrated its excellence.
Together, these studies, which are summarized in Table
12, demonstrate the power and versatility of conditional
diffusion models in an extremely broad range of restoration
tasks, ranging from environmental restoration to biomedical
imaging, which illustrates their role as a new paradigm in
image restoration research.

 VII. HUMAN POSTURE AND MOVEMENT MODELING
 Human posture and movement modeling and forecasting are
of central interest to areas like ergonomics, human-computer
interaction, computer animation and autonomous systems.
Recent advances in generative modeling, particularly with
conditional diffusion models, have opened new doors for
capturing the inherently stochastic and complicated human
movement with increased realism, expressiveness and inter-
pretability.
One of the interesting applications in occupational health
was presented in [72], where conditional diffusion models
were employed to predict workers’ postures while carrying
out manual material handling tasks. The intention was to
minimize musculoskeletal disorder (MSD) risk by predict-
ing posture variation in real-world settings. Using U-Net
and multilayer perceptron (MLP) architectures trained on
anatomical landmark data, the diffusion-based approach had
very good predictive accuracy and could capture natural
human variation, especially with the MLP, opening up an
interesting path for personalized ergonomic assessment and
workplace design optimization.
Complementing the focus on physical posture, [73] intro-
duced DiffAR, a novel human activity recognition (HAR)
method that does not require traditional sensors or cam-
eras. Instead, it employed WiFi-based channel state infor-
mation (CSI) and an Adaptive Conditional Diffusion Model
(ACDM) to produce robust CSI representations. The model
avoided limitations of rigid time windows and missing data
and significantly improved HAR performance if combined
with an ensemble classifier. The paper illustrates how dif-
fusion models can be employed to enhance unobtrusive,
infrastructure-free activity recognition systems in real-world
settings.
From still poses to movement trajectories, the work in
[74] introduced the Quantized Conditional Diffusion Model
(QCDM) for predicting future motion trajectories that reflect
the randomness present in human activities. The two-stage
framework added a Discrete Motion Quantization Module
and a Conditional Motion Generation Module and employed
GCNs and Transformers for encoding temporal dynamics
and action-specific context. A diversity generation mecha-
nism also facilitated the generation of a high quantity of
realistic motion sequences beyond deterministic baselines in
motion realism and diversity.
Subsequent to this, [75] developed DivDiff, a model that
combined denoising diffusion probabilistic modeling with
Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) and Transformer-based
encodings to generate diverse but anatomically realistic hu-
man motion. The work centered around the Diversified Re-
inforcement Sampling Function (DRSF), which encouraged
generation in the direction of physically coherent output with
guarantees of diversity. Benchmarks on benchmark datasets
ensured DivDiff’s success in achieving a balance between
realism and diversity, pushing the state of motion prediction
tasks.
Scaling to sign language production, [76] introduced a
Gloss-driven Conditional Diffusion Model (GCDM) that was
able to produce sign language gestures from text or audio
inputs. The model encoded gloss sequences as a Transformer
encoder and integrated semantic priors into sign pose gen-
eration by diffusion modeling. Multiple gesture hypotheses
were generated and averaged at inference time to produce
high-confidence sign language videos. Experiments on the
Phoenix2014T dataset indicated the good performance of
both qualitative and quantitative nature of the model, indi-
cating its feasibility for assistive communication devices.
Finally, addressing problems of gesture recognition when
under occlusion, [77] proposed DiffTrans, a diffusion frame-
work designed to recover lost skeletal data. Casting the
problem of occlusion handling as conditional denoising,
DiffTrans generated realistic imputations for missing joints
and significantly improved gesture recognition accuracy even

Collectively, these works (an overview is shown in Table
13) illustrate the adaptability and generative capability of
conditional diffusion models in human posture and motion
analysis. From occupational health to wireless sensing, mo-
tion prediction, sign language generation or occlusion-robust
recognition, diffusion models yield a robust and physically
grounded paradigm to render and produce human motion in
a more sophisticated, diverse and responsive form.
 VIII. INTELLIGENT TRANSPORTATION SYSTEMS
 Recent advances of conditional diffusion models have sig-
nificantly contributed to traffic and transportation research,
solving a broad set of issues from state estimation to data im-
putation, trajectory forecasting and urban network modeling,
as shown in Table 14.
Lei et al. [78] addressed the issue of traffic state estimation
in sensor-free regions by proposing CDSTE, a Conditional
Diffusion-based Spatio-Temporal Estimator. CDSTE merged
conditional diffusion with spatio-temporal neural networks
to provide reliable probabilistic estimates that improved
more adaptable and robust traffic management. Experimental
comparisons demonstrated that CDSTE typically performed
better than five widely used baselines.
To this, Wu et al. [79] focused on enhancing data quality
in transportation networks that are marred by missing or
noisy inputs. They proposed STCDM, a Spatio-Temporal
Transformer combined with a Conditional Diffusion Model
and effectively combined graph-based traffic structure and
temporal attention mechanisms. The resultant hybrid model
achieved up to a 1.11% increase in imputation accuracy based
on public traffic datasets compared to other solutions.
In addition to state estimation and data recovery, condi-
tional diffusion has also been effective in vehicle trajectory
prediction. Li et al. [80] developed a coarse-to-fine trajec-
tory prediction pipeline in which a Conditional Variational
Autoencoder (CVAE) was employed initially to produce
trajectory proposals, which were later conditioned with a
conditional diffusion model. For the treatment of data spar-
sity and irregular sampling, trajectories were projected onto
the Frenet coordinate system and the lane-aware attention
mechanism guided prediction. Their method achieved im-
proved performance on Argoverse and nuScenes with im-
proved balance of accuracy and efficiency in computation and
successful application in urban field tests.
Similarly, Liu et al. [81] introduced TrajDiffuse, a guided
conditional diffusion model optimized for accurate and var-
ied trajectory forecasting. By framing the task as an inpaint-
ing of trajectories with map-based guidance, TrajDiffuse
achieved high fidelity to environmental constraints while still
ensuring diversity and collision-free behavior. NuScenes and
PFSD benchmarks established its advantage over state-of-
the-art baselines.
From forecasting to generative planning, Gu et al. [82]
proposed an image-based urban road network generation
method through conditional diffusion. The model generated
realistic road patterns under four context factors (terrain,
land use, etc.) while maintaining both natural hindrances and
human rules of design. Experiment on five cities in America
proved the model can generate realistic and geographically
coherent road networks and intersections are found to be a
driving factor.
Based on the use of generative models in urban science,
Shi et al. [83] tackled the prediction of urban morphology
from local geographic and socioeconomic characteristics.
Departing from GAN-based approaches, they employed a
score-based conditional diffusion model that decomposed
the problem into conditional gradient estimation and itera-
tive sampling. This alleviated the need for assuming fixed
probability distributions and captured more complex spatial
patterns, yielding considerable improvements in pixel-level,
shallow and deep structural features (5.5%, 5.9% and 13.2%
respectively).
The work [84] introduced a diffusion-guided seman-
tic bird-eye-view (BEV) map generation network with a
boundary-aware loss function to address class imbalance
for autonomous driving scene perception. The sensory data
imbalance collected with road layouts dominating and road
objects as minority might lead to unsatisfactory BEV map
generation performance. By increasing the weightage of mi-
nority classes during learning, the new network attempted to
promote learning samples for minority objects. Experimental
results showed that the new approach performed better than
existing methods and effectively alleviated the class imbal-
ance issue.
 IX. MECHANICS AND ENGINEERING
 CDMs are a novel, generalizable family of generative models
that have attracted much interest from the mechanics and
engineering societies in recent times. They exhibit remark-
able sensitivity in usage in simulation, inverse design, quality
control, prediction and anomaly detection applications. With
their ability to represent high-dimensional, intricate distribu-
tions and imbue physical constraints and multi-modal data,
these models have enabled researchers to tackle time-worn
problems with increased accuracy and versatility in various
domains, as outlined in Table 15.
Starting from fluid dynamics, researchers [24] introduced
a probabilistic diffusion-based approach that was capable of
generating turbulent flow fields under different physical con-
ditions. Employing Bayesian sampling with autoregressive
gradient-based conditioning, their framework could generate
high-fidelity long-span flows and facilitate smooth URANS-
to-LES simulation transitions. This work takes computational
fluid dynamics one step further by reducing the computa-
tional cost of resolving fine-scale turbulence.
From this simulation capability, CDMs have shown a lot
of capability in materials science, particularly in inverse
design of complex structures. The authors [85] presented

MOFFUSION, a latent diffusion model for designing metal-
organic frameworks (MOFs), with signed distance functions
(SDFs) to describe complex porous geometries in a versatile
manner. The model handled multimodal input data and out-
performed traditional approaches in designing materials with
targeted properties. Similarly, the researchers [23] were able
to surmount the issue of sparse data in additive manufactur-
ing by developing a 3D Conditional Diffusion Model (3D-
CDM). Through a topological perturbation-based augmenta-
tion approach, they augmented a small dataset and trained
a generative model that produced structurally diverse and
functionally stable metamaterial designs that outperformed
voxel-based baselines.
CDMs have also proven useful in quality control, espe-
cially in precision manufacture. For instance, the authors [86]
designed a Multi-Scale Conditional Diffusion Model (MS-
CDM) for coherence scanning interferometry (CSI) signal
recovery from contamination during OLED production. Us-
ing a self-supervised learning method, the model accurately
estimated droplet volumes with low error levels, showing
improved performance in signal recovery and confirming the
use of CDMs in precision control environments.
Beyond process and material design, CDMs are emerging
to be used in system monitoring and predictive maintenance.
For structural health monitoring (SHM), the authors [87]
developed DF-CDM, a frequency-domain data-integrated su-
pervised denoising networks model to reconstruct dynamic
responses of civil infrastructure. Used on a three-span bridge,
DF-CDM performed significantly better than GAN-based
models, with its potential to be applied for real-time diag-
nostics and damage detection.
CDMs are addressing forecasting and privacy problems

in energy networks. The authors [88] presented DiffPLF, a
diffusion model for probabilistic electric vehicle (EV) charg-
ing demand forecasting. The model effectively integrated
cross-attention mechanisms and task-informed fine-tuning
and well-represented variability in charging and forecast
accuracy over baselines. Synergistically, Wang et al. [89] pro-
posed a privacy-preserving CDM that produced realistic and
customer-specific electricity load profiles even in situations
where data is scant. Stacked residual and attention layers
were employed by their model to facilitate high-quality gen-
eration while maintaining data confidentiality.
The robustness and controllability of CDMs also have
been used in fault diagnosis. Researchers [90] introduced
VGCDM, a pulse voltage-guided diffusion model for high-
speed rail (HSR) bogie systems. To address instability is-
sues common in GANs, VGCDM used a sequential U-Net
architecture and cross-attention mechanisms to align control
signals with vibration information. The model demonstrated
accurate generation of conditional vibration signals even at
varying operational speeds.
In industrial settings, sensor missing data can severely
degrade model reliability. To alleviate this, the authors [91]
proposed a light-weight CDM model with a customized
imputation approach and soft feedback mechanism for trust-
worthy sensor recovery. Tested on nickel smelting and power
plant system datasets, the approach significantly improved
downstream model performance and training efficiency.
CDMs also exhibit excellent performance in handling
multivariate time series for Internet of Things (IoT) applica-
tions. The authors [92] proposed MAFCD, a Multi-level and
Adaptive Conditional Diffusion model, which is particularly
developed for industrial time series anomaly detection. By
dynamically adjusting feature fusion weights and ensemble
aggregation, MAFCD achieved state-of-the-art performance
on several industrial applications, including chemical manu-
facturing processes.
Expanding the scope of energy systems modeling even
further, Zhao et al. [93] suggested CDSG, a conditional
diffusion-based Scenario Generation, to address renewable
energy generation and consumption uncertainty issues. With
the assistance of an expert noise prediction network incor-
porating spatio-temporal correlation modules, CDSG effec-
tively generated realistic, diverse and controllable source-
load scenarios. Its use in optimal power dispatch simulations
demonstrated its worth in deep decarbonization planning.
Finally, in mechanical design, Zhang et al. [22] developed
LatticeOptDiff, a diffusion-based inverse design method to
design lattice structures with target mechanical properties
such as Young’s modulus, Poisson’s ratio and volume frac-
tion. The method outperformed GANs for state-of-the-art
performance in designing high-performance unit cells, as val-
idated by finite element analysis and 3D-printed prototypes.
The work [94] described why Non-intrusive Load Mon-
itoring (NILM) is important for the analysis of energy
consumption in homes without individual metering of ap-
pliances. The study suggested a new framework called

The study [95] explored using a conditional diffusion
model in deep learning for the prediction of heat transfer
during casting, instead of numerical simulation. The model
was trained on geometry shapes, initial temperature fields
and temperature fields at some time points with random
noise as input. Accuracy in predicting temperature fields in
a single time step was 97.7% and for sequential time steps
was 69.1%, with errors occurring in the sand mold. Shape
of geometry was seen to have greater influence on prediction
accuracy than initial temperature field, since the former could
distinguish between casting, mold and chill on the basis of
color. Overall, the diffusion model had potential to serve as a
numerical simulation proxy in the casting process.
The study [96] addressed the issue of generating realis-
tic speckle images to be used by digital image correlation
(DIC) algorithms. Traditional methods struggled to accu-
rately mimic brightness variations and were computationally
demanding. The authors proposed a high-fidelity method
with a conditional diffusion model to generate DIC speckle
images with cracks and offered spatial and spectral domain-
based evaluation metrics. The model functioned well in
applications such as crack image segmentation and speckle
image generation, performing outstandingly in the latter. The
proposed metrics facilitated thorough analysis of synthetic-
natural speckle image registration. The study suggested that
this approach would enhance the robustness and accuracy
of DIC technology in mechanical testing and engineering
applications.
Collectively, these innovations confirm the revolutionary
potential of CDMs in engineering. CDMs offer one uni-
fied framework that supports high-fidelity simulation, data-
efficient design, robust monitoring and privacy-preserving
forecasting. Their capacity to support heterogeneous data
sources, allow for uncertainty modeling and generate phys-
ically correct outputs makes them fundamental enablers of
next-generation intelligent engineering systems.
 X. SECURITY APPLICATIONS: ATTACKS, DEFENSE
AND PRIVACY
 Recent research showcases the growing impact of CDMs
in machine learning security, where they are both power-
ful defense mechanisms and sophisticated adversarial attack
tools. The models have been especially potent in use cases
ranging from adversarial defense and model inversion to pri-
vacy protection and data anonymization. In this section, the
most prominent security applications of CDMs are presented,
discussed and summarized in Table 16
For adversarial defense, Shi et al. [97] presented a Gen-
erative Adversarial Defense (GAD) approach founded on
CDMs. Unlike traditional methods such as adversarial train-
ing or input preprocessing, GAD is model-agnostic and
seeks to reclaim adversarial examples to their clean versions.
Through the conditioning of the reverse diffusion process
on class or content information, GAD enhances robustness
along with perceptual fidelity. Empirical experiments showed
that GAD significantly outperforms previous defenses, set-
ting a new state of the art for adversarial robustness in both
visual quality and classification accuracy.
Diffusion models can be not only applied to defend adver-
sarial attacks but also used to generate adversarial attacks.
Liu et al. [98] proposed the Conditional Diffusion Model
Attack (CDMA), which is a black-box attack framework
that efficiently produces adversarial examples through condi-
tional denoising diffusion. By parameterizing the adversarial
example as a transformation of the benign input under a
learned conditional distribution, CDMA greatly reduces the
number of queries, with attack success rates above 99%,
typically with a single query. CDMA surpasses nine state-of-
the-art black-box attack methods consistently, demonstrating
the offensive capabilities of diffusion-based systems.
Other than perturbation attacks, conditional diffusion has
been used in model inversion attacks (MIAs) as well. Liu
et al. [99] demonstrated that it is possible to recover repre-
sentative inputs for a target label despite black-box or label-
only access. Their method is to use an auxiliary dataset and
label guidance to train a diffusion model to generate plausible
inputs, outperforming existing inversion methods and raising
serious model privacy leakage issues.
In addition to adversarial attacks, conditional diffusion
models also open up new avenues for privacy-preserving ap-
plications, including facial de-identification, medical imag-
ing and private data sharing. The models can selectively
alter private features (e.g., identity, face shape) while leav-
ing contextual information like pose, expression or scene
context intact, thus providing a trade-off between utility and
anonymity.
Shaheryar et al. [25] presented an Identity Diffuser, a two-
conditional diffusion model, which anonymizes face images
in public areas with retention of salient task-relevant charac-
teristics (e.g., emotion). It employs synthetic identities and
disentangles identity and non-identity features in a special-
ized latent space. It ensures temporal coherence among video
frames and does not need outside feature extractors. The
approach led to the improvement of emotion recognition
performance, image quality under extreme poses and output
diversity, demonstrating its potential for secure deployment
in surveillance and computer vision systems.
In the healthcare domain, Wang et al. [26] proposed the
Medical Semantic Diffusion Model (MSDM) for medical
image generation with no personally identifiable information
(PII). MSDM uses Adaptive Batch Normalization to repre-
sent semantic structures in latent space and incorporates a
Spread Algorithm for semantic mask generation automati-

These advances illustrate the double-edged nature of

tect models from attack through robust reconstruction and
privacy-preserving generation. On the other hand, they also
enable potent attacks, from low-query adversarial genera-
tion to high-fidelity model inversion. Their modularity and
capacity to learn complex data distributions make CDMs a
key frontier for both attacking and defending modern deep
learning systems.
 XI. OTHER APPLICATIONS
 CDMs have demonstrated staggering diversity beyond stan-
dard image generation, achieving state-of-the-art perfor-
mance in a broad variety of applications such as recom-
mendation systems, object detection, speech synthesis, image
reconstruction and scientific computing. Below are some of
the most fascinating applications, grouped by domain.
 A. DESIGN FIELD
 CDMs are increasingly being used as design drivers in as
varied as architecture, materials, and engineering. CDMs in
aerodynamics couple airfoil shape conditioned by target per-
formance, and realistic smoothing to enable downstream flow
analysis [100]. In architecture and urban planning, control-
augmented pipelines and conditional latent diffusion push
generated layouts into compliance with structural constraints
and enable near–real-time iteration [101], [102]. Interior
design study further integrates form and function by curation
of domain-specific data sets and incorporation of composite
losses for style, spatial functionality and aesthetics, with
batch generation and editability at pace [103], [104]. Beyond
form-finding, CDMs also facilitate multi-objective digital
material design, where micro-layout is optimized to meet
multiple mechanical goals in parallel [105]. Overall, these
results indicate high application potential and market demand
for controllable, constraint-sensitive generative pipelines in
commercial design practice.
 B. RECOMMENDATION SYSTEMS
 Chen et al. [106] presented a conditional diffusion archi-
tecture for enhancing personalization and mitigating infor-
mation overload in recommendation systems. By incorpo-
rating user interaction vectors as conditioning signals into
the reverse diffusion process, the model achieved profound
improvements in areas like movies, music, beauty and sports.
Specifically, precision metrics were enhanced by 7.41% and
6.00% and Top-10 and Top-20 recommendation correctness
was enhanced by 5.59% and 4.38%, respectively. Sensitivity
analysis also reflected the usefulness of small diffusion steps
and modest levels of noise.
 C. CAMOUFLAGED OBJECT DETECTION
 On the Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) front, Sun et
al. [107] introduced CamoDiffusion , a condition diffusion-
based method towards precise mask generation. The model
merged an adaptive transformer-condition module with a
denoising model and used variance noise scheduling and
structure corruption mechanisms. In a bid to check overcon-
fidence in prediction, a Consensus Time Ensemble mecha-
nism was suggested. Empirical evaluations confirmed that
CamoDiffusion surpassed previous COD and salient object
detection methods and a VQ-VAE-based implementation en-
abled faster inference.
 D. SPEECH SYNTHESIS
 CDMs offer an effective method for high-fidelity speech
synthesis using conditioning on textual or phonetic inputs
to recover waveforms or spectrograms. Huang et al. [108]
proposed FastDiff , a time-conscious convolution-based ac-
celerated conditional diffusion model with a learned predic-
tor of the noise schedule. Embedded in an end-to-end text-
to-speech (TTS) system ( FastDiff-TTS ), the model achieved
a Mean Opinion Score (MOS) of 4.28, demonstrating natural
 20 VOLUME 4, 2016

 and expressive audio output with satisfactory sampling effi-
ciency and high generalizability to novel data.
 E. LOW-RESOURCE IMAGE SYNTHESIS
 Lei et al. [109] presented EDG-CDM , an encoder-
conditioned conditional diffusion model, as a response to
challenges in image generation under low-resource settings.
The encoder was pre-trained on contrastive objectives and
noise-aware KL divergence, followed by fine-tuning in a
supervised setting for class-aware conditioning. Experimen-
tation on benchmark datasets confirmed its high performance
with regard to Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Incep-
tion Scores, indicating its stability in low-resource settings.
 F. HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGING
 Si et al. [68] introduced CASSIDiff , the first diffusion-based
approach to hyperspectral cube reconstruction in Coded
Aperture Snapshot Spectral Imaging (CASSI) systems. The
model also prioritized perceptual quality with LPIPS and FID
scores over traditional MSE and PSNR. The model combined
wavelet-based feature fusion and spatial-spectral attention
with the aim of enhancing consistency and denoising. Exper-
imental results on synthetic and real data sets demonstrated
its excellence.
 G. DOMAIN ADAPTATION
 Zhang et al. [110] proposed the Domain-guided Conditional
Diffusion Model (DCDM) to improve performance on Unsu-
pervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) tasks. DCDM generated
class-controlled target-domain samples and employed a do-
main classifier to guide diffusion. The approach successfully
addressed large domain shifts, significantly improving target-
domain accuracy.
 H. INTERACTIVE ART AND COLORIZATION
 In artistic applications, Carrillo et al. [111] developed an in-
teractive line-art colorization interface using conditional dif-
fusion. The model incorporated user-provided color strokes
through a coupled conditioning framework, generating di-
verse and visually appealing outputs. FID, LPIPS and SSIM
metrics confirmed its advantage over existing methods.
 I. PANSHARPENING
 To address spectral distortion in pansharpening, Zhang et
al. [112] introduced FrDiff , a DDPM-based model that pre-
serves spectral details compromised in spatially-oriented
methods. It utilized framelet-based embeddings and cross-
attention modules to maintain spectral fidelity. Benchmark
experiments verified its stability and improved image quality.
 J. IMAGE TRANSMISSION OVER NOISY CHANNELS
 Yang et al. [28] employed conditional diffusion models
for joint source-channel coding (JSCC) of robust image
transmission. Their model employed entropy models for
bandwidth-quality trade-offs and a conditional diffusion de-
coder for image reconstruction from symbols. On the basis
of a mamba-like fast linear attention mechanism, the model
outperformed conventional JSCC methods, obtaining percep-
tually superior reconstructions.
 K. SCIENTIFIC COMPUTING AND DYNAMICAL
SYSTEMS
 For simulating complex physical systems, Dong et al. [113]
combined CDMs with neural operators for building non-
local stochastic closure models for partial differential equa-
tions (PDEs). Through the integration of the Fourier Neural
Operator into a score-based diffusion system, the approach
enabled multiscale simulation with faster sampling, which
is an enormous advancement in scientific simulation under
uncertainty.
 L. INVERSE PROBLEMS
 Chung et al. [114] addressed the inefficiency of vanilla diffu-
sion models in inverse problem-solving with the introduction
of Come-Closer-Diffuse-Faster (CCDF). This initialization
technique significantly reduced sampling steps without loss
of performance. CCDF achieved state-of-the-art performance
on super-resolution, inpainting and MRI reconstruction tasks,
consolidating speed and performance within a single frame-
work.
 XII. APPLICATION-WISE SYNTHESIS AND DISCUSSION
 We synthesize patterns within each application scenario
along four axes: problem framing, evidence synthesis across
papers, failure modes & external validity and practical con-
clusions.
 A. MEDICAL IMAGING AND CLINICAL WORKFLOWS
 Problem framing: CDMs are utilized in segmentation
conditioning, artifact reduction, and modality fusion/super-
resolution under regulatory and data-scarcity restraints [12]–
[15], [31], [37], [38].
 Evidence synthesis: Weakly/fully supervised conditional
pipelines boost structure compliance and task performance:
segmentation-aware generation boosts downstream Dice and
HD95 [12], [14]; degradation-guided conditioning reduces
CT metal artifacts [15]; tri-modal fusion and semantic 3D
synthesis show that multi-branch conditioning improves
cross-modality fidelity [31], [37]. Across the literature, con-
ditioning strength and compliance measures (Dice/HD95,
AUROC) are more predictive of clinical performance than
collective perceptual measures alone.
 Failure modes and external validity: Performance worsens
under distribution change (scanner/site) and noisy control
hides; over-smoothing and hallucination risk when guidance
is strong or data are scarce [13]. Reproducibility depends
on reporting seeds/samplers and releasing precomputed fea-
tures.
 Practical conclusions: (i) Use condition-adherence mea-
surements (Dice/HD95) over FID-alone reporting; (ii) use
domain priors (anatomical masks, degradation models) dur-
ing training and inference; (iii) validate across sites to capture

 shift; (iv) choose latent pipelines when compute/latency bud-
gets are limited [7].
 B. REMOTE SENSING AND ASTROPHYSICS
 Problem framing: Challenges include super-resolution, de-
speckling, SAR ⇐ optical conversion and cosmological/astro
inference with strong physical priors [16]–[19], [32], [51],
[52], [55], [59].
 Evidence synthesis: Reference-based SR is improved
with conditioning on change priors [51]; spatiotemporal
fusion with CDMs improves temporal coherence [52];
Fourier/attention hybridization reduces artifacts in RS-SR
[16], [17]; SAR tasks are assisted by spatial–frequency re-
finement and despeckling-aware objectives [18], [19]. In
astrophysics, CDMs facilitate lensing SR and spectra infer-
ence from images, making them indicative of science-grade
pipelines when used in conjunction with domain metrics
[32], [55].
 Failure modes and external validity: Hallucinated ge-
ometries can happen in RS scenes with dense textures; out-
of-distribution land covers degrade cFID. Physics-violating
outputs are caused by losses that ignore sensor or noise
models.
 Practical conclusions: (i) Always use FID/IS along with
task/physics metrics (PSNR/SSIM + land-cover IoU; lensing
SR quality); (ii) include sensor/noise priors in conditioning;
(iii) report per-class/region cFID to reveal coverage; (iv) use
ControlNet-style structural inputs if maps (edges/seg/depth)
are present [10].
 C. MECHANICS, MATERIALS AND ENGINEERING
 Problem framing: Applications cover turbulence genera-
tion, inverse material/metamaterial design, manufacturing
metrology, SHM and energy/load modeling [23], [24], [85]–
[89].
 Evidence synthesis: Bayesian CDMs generate turbulence
fields that bridge URANS ⇒ LES gaps [24]; multi-modal con-
ditional pipelines drive MOF and metamaterial inverse de-
sign [23], [85]; manufacturing quality inspection is facilitated
by self-supervised CDMs for interferometry signal recov-
ery [86]. In infrastructure, denoising/fusion improves SHM
signal quality [87]. Energy forecasting and synthetic load
generation illustrate CDMs can encode uncertainty while
preserving privacy and operational constraints [88], [89].
 Failure modes and external validity: Physics viola-
tions and unstable long-horizon behavior occur without con-
straints; data leakage and narrow operating regimes inflate
apparent gains.
 Practical conclusions: (i) Pair generation with physics or
constraints (e.g., PDE-informed losses, feasibility checks);
(ii) report downstream KPIs (e.g., drag/lift, strength, forecast
error) in addition to perceptual scores; (iii) publish ablations
on sampler steps/guidance to expose cost–quality Pareto
fronts.
 D. HUMAN POSTURE AND MOTION
 Problem framing: CDMs are used for posture prediction,
HAR with alternative sensing, diverse motion synthesis, sign-
language production and occlusion-robust recognition [72]–
[77].
 Evidence synthesis: Conditioning on skeletons or land-
marks yields ergonomic posture prediction [72]; WiFi-
CSI + adaptive conditioning = sensor-free HAR [73];
quantized/Transformer-augmented CDMs improve motion
diversity and plausibility [74], [75]; gloss-conditioned mod-
els create fluent sign sequences [76]. In occlusion-robust
recognition, CDMs impute missing joints and boost robust-
ness [77].
 Failure modes and external validity: Domain changes
(subject, environment) and long-horizon drift stress compli-
ance; safety-critical deployment requires constraint checking
(joint limits, collision).
 Practical conclusions: (i) Monitor compliance with kine-
matic validity and task metrics (MPJPE, FID-k, recognition
AUROC); (ii) inject priors (skeleton limits, dynamics) to
regularize long sequences; (iii) report per-subject/per-view
breakdowns to expose generalization.
 E. SECURITY, PRIVACY AND ML ROBUSTNESS
 Problem framing: CDMs now take place on both attack and
defense sides of ML security: defenses that recover clean
inputs and attacks/inversions that steal or mislead models
[25], [26], [97]–[99].
 Evidence synthesis: Model-agnostic defenses remove ad-
versarial inputs without losing semantics [97]; black-box
attacks employ conditional paths to obtain high success
at low queries [98]; label-only inversions expose privacy
risks [99]. Privacy-preserving generators provide PII-free or
anonymized images with maintained task utility [25], [26].
 Failure modes and external validity: Adversaries who
adapt can evade diffuser priors; de-identification may fail on
edge cases. Defense gains can be forfeit under new threat
models unless rigorously tested.
 Practical conclusions: (i) Implement robustness across a
broad spectrum of threat models and budgets; (ii) combine
generative defenses with detection/verification; (iii) assess
privacy–utility trade-offs through standardized downstream
tasks.
 F. CROSS-CUTTING CONCLUSIONS
 Controllability prevails over unconditional quality:
 Across domains, condition adherence and downstream per-
formance outscore FID alone [7], [8], [10], [29].
 Domain priors aid stability: Physics/sensor/anatomical
priors or structural controls (seg/pose/depth), reduce drift and
hallucination [10], [15], [18], [24].
 Report Pareto, not points: Sweeping sampler steps and
guidance unveil deployable operating points; per-condition
cFID reveals coverage shortfall.
We recommend assessing CDMs on (i) explicit condition
adherence, (ii) domain/task KPIs and (iii) cost/latency at

 XIII. CONCLUSION
 CDMs are proposed as a strong and general class of gener-
ative models able to address any type of task in computer
vision, remote sensing, urban modeling and more. By ex-
ploiting the flexibility of diffusion processes along with the
conditioning mechanisms, CDMs facilitate the generation of
controlled, rich and high-quality data even from incomplete,
noisy or ambiguous input.
This survey paper provided a comprehensive synopsis of
the current progress made in CDMs, dividing the literature
by application domains and illustrating architectural inno-
vations, conditioning methods, as well as empirical per-
formance. We illustrated the ways in which CDMs have
surpassed traditional and even pre-deep learning approaches
in image restoration, trajectory prediction and traffic state
estimation tasks, offering both interpretability and resilience.
While their growing success, CDMs also face several chal-
lenges. Table 17 lists the primary challenges , future direc-
tions and suggested solutions of CDMs. Key challenges are
high computational costs, low generalizability to real-world
environments and weak theoretical foundations, especially
conditional consistency. The table shows that enhancing in-
ference techniques such as DDIM or progressive distillation
would fill performance gaps. Along with this, methods like
domain adaptation and robust training are brought to the fore-
front for real-world application improvement. The research
also seeks theoretical progress and improved modality fusion
processes to manage challenges in multi-modal conditioning.
Training scale-up and efficiency are countered by archi-
tectural breakthroughs like transformer-based models and
parameter-efficient training. Lastly, integrating CDMs into
end-to-end application workflows is brought to the forefront
as a critical step towards improving their applied utility.
Practitioner recommendations:
 • Report per-condition metrics: report cFID and adher-
ence scores (e.g., m IoU/PCK/text–image similarity)
alongside FID/IS [7], [8], [10], [29].
 • Plot quality–cost curves: sweep sampler steps and guid-
ance to expose Pareto frontiers and select deployment
operating points.
 • Condition harder: pre-validate control maps (Canny/depth/
pose/seg.) and use domain-calibrated priors where avail-
able [10], [15], [18].
 • Measure where it matters: use downstream task metrics
(Dice/HD95, AUROC, Chamfer, engn/physics KPIs) in
domain adoption [12], [24], [33].
 • Make it replicable: publish code, configs, prompts/ con-
ditions and (where permissible) feature stats; fix seeds
and system versions.
Critical gaps are: strong adherence during extreme distribu-
tion shift (extreme poses/layouts, out-of-spec sensors), cost-
conscious training/inference (distillation, consistency mod-
els, efficient samplers) for high-res outputs [8], physics- and
safety-conscious objectives that combine domain constraints
and generation (e.g., turbulence, SAR, medical) [12], [18],
[24] and security/privacy when generative defenses and at-
tacks co-evolve [25], [26], [98], [99]. We anticipate continued
convergence of adapterized control (e.g., ControlNet vari-
ants), multimodal priors and efficient samplers, with metrics
centered on adherence and operational utility.
In the future, we also anticipate upcoming work to focus on
hybrid architectures that combine diffusion with other mod-
els (e.g., transformers or VAEs), faster sampling algorithms,
improved multi-modal conditioning and deeper embedding
within task-specific pipelines. Beyond that, continued theo-
retical development of CDMs and their optimization land-
scapes will be critical to seeing them fully realized.
With increasing growth in work in conditional diffusion
models, we hope this review can serve as a helpful in-
troduction for researchers and practitioners seeking to un-
derstand and contribute significantly to this continuously
evolving field. By synthesizing key developments, challenges
and opportunities, we aim to provide a solid foundation for
future exploration and innovation in conditional generative
modeling.

 THEODOR PANAGIOTAKOPOULOS received his diploma, Ph.D. and M.Sc. degrees in Com- puter Science from the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Patras in 2006, 2011 and 2020 respectively. He is cur- rently an Assistant Professor in the Department of Management Science and Technology at the University of Patras, specializing in Internet of Things applications. Since 2011, he has been a research fellow in the Laboratory of Mobile and Pervasive Computing, Quality and Ambient Intelligence of the Hellenic University and since 2020, a visiting professor at the University of Nicosia. His research interests include pervasive systems, cloud platforms, machine learning and Internet of Things systems, technologies and applications, with a focus on smart cities, energy and healthcare. Additionally, his research activities target continuous professional training in key emerging digital technologies through e-learning frameworks. He has published more than 80 scientific papers in reputable international journals and conferences. He has also participated in more than 30 European and national research projects (e.g., H2020, Horizon Europe, Erasmus+), holding key roles at research, technical and managerial levels.
 SOTIRIS KOTSIANTIS eceived his B.Sc., M.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees in Computer Science from the University of Patras, Greece, in 1999, 2001 and 2005, respectively. With a background in Mathe- matics, he currently serves as an Associate Profes- sor in the Department of Mathematics at the Uni- versity of Patras. According to Google Scholar, he has an H-index of 47 and a G-index of 171, reflecting the impact of his extensive publication record in international journals and conferences. His research interests focus on data mining, machine learning and learning analytics.
 ALEXANDROS GKILLAS received his Diploma from the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Patras, Greece. He also completed both his MSc, PhD from the Computer Engineering and Informatics Depart- ment (CEID) at the same university. Since July 2021, he has been a member of the Industrial Sys- tems Institute at Athena Research Center. In June 2023, Alexandros began working as a Computer Vision Engineer at AVISense.AI and in September 2024, he started as a Postdoc Researcher at the Industrial Systems Institute. He has contributed to several Horizon EU and national projects, advancing AI and computer vision technologies. His broader scientific interests include signal and image processing, explainable AI, deep learning and their appli- cations to emerging challenges in autonomous driving.
 ARIS S. LALOS received the Diploma, M.A.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees from the Computer Engineer- ing and Informatics Department, University of Patras (UoP), Rio-Patras, Greece, in 2003, 2005 and 2010, respectively. He is currently a Research Director at Industrial Systems Institute of Athena Research Center (ATHENA R.C.). He has been a Senior Research Scientist at the Signal Processing and Communications Laboratory, CEID, SE, from 2005 to 2010; at the Signal Theory and Commu- nications (TSC) Department, Technical University of Catalonia, Barcelona, Spain, from October 2012 to December 2014 and at the Visualization and Virtual Reality Group of the Electrical and Computer Engineering depart- ment, UoP, from Jan 2015 to Jun. 2018. From October 2011 to October 2012, he was a Telecommunication Research Engineer at Analogies S. A., an early stage starts up. In May 2018, he was elected as a Principal Researcher and in Feb. 2023 as a Research Director at Industrial Systems Institute, ATHENA R.C.. He is the author of 170 research papers in international journals (53), conferences (108) and book chapters (9). He has participated in 25 European and National projects related to robotics, precision agriculture, autonomous vehicles and e-health domains. His general research interests include model based deep learning, 2D/3D scene analysis, distributed signal processing and learning over graphs .He received the Best Demo Award in IEEE CAMAD 2014, the Best Paper Award in IEEE ISSPIT 2015 and the World’s FIRST 10K Best Paper Award in IEEE ICME 2017. He acts as a regular reviewer of several technical journals. In January 2015, he was nominated as an Exemplary Reviewer of the IEEE COMMUNICATIONS LETTERS. He served as a Deputy Coordinator for the CPSoSAware H2020 EU Project and as a Technical Coordinator for the GamECAR H2020 EU Project. Furthermore, he had the role of Work Package Leader in five H2020 Projects. After 2018, he formed his own group (https://mips.isi.gr) within ISI that now counts ten active members (post-docs, Ph.D. students and programming engineers) in research and development projects. Since 2019, he is also the president of the scientific advisory board of Industrial Systems Institute. Finally, in June 2023 he co-founded AviSense.AI, a spin off of ATHENA R.C. and UoP that brings forth perception technologies that bolster safety within the broad consumer vehicle market.

 EfficientTransformer: A Dynamic Anomaly
Detection Model for Industrial Control Networks
 JINYANG LIU 1,2 , GUOGANG WANG 1,2 , XUEJUN ZONG 1,2 , BOWEI NING 2 , AND KAN HE 1,2 1 College of Information Engineering, Shenyang University of Chemical Technology, Shenyang, Liaoning 110142, China 2 Key Laboratory of Information Security for Petrochemical Industry, Shenyang, Liaoning 110142, China
Corresponding author: Xuejun Zong (xuejun_zong@syuct.edu.cn)
This work was supported in part by the Science and Technology Project of Liaoning Province of China under Grant 2023JH1/10400082, in part the by the Science and Technology Major Project of Liaoning Province of China under Grant [2024] 4(3), and in part by the Science and Technology Innovation Program in Artificial Intelligence of Liaoning Province of China under Grant 2023JH26/1030008.
 ABSTRACT As industrial control network threats become increasingly complex, traditional intrusion
detection systems (IDS) struggle to capture implicit relationships due to feature redundancy and intricate
feature interactions. This leads to increased computational complexity and higher detection latency, making
it difficult for industrial control systems(ICS) to meet the fast and accurate response requirements for
security events. In this study, we propose a dynamic anomaly detection model for industrial control
networks, named EfficientTransformer. The model uses a 1D Convolutional Neural Network (1D-CNN)
to extract local features from the data, while a linear multi-head self-attention mechanism, replacing
the traditional Transformer’s multi-head attention mechanism, provides global learning capabilities. This
reduces computational complexity and enables efficient parallel learning. Additionally, to address the issue
of class imbalance, the model incorporates a weighted cross-entropy loss function that assigns higher weights
to the minority class of abnormal traffic, thereby improving the model’s anomaly detection ability. This
innovation further mitigates issues of feature redundancy and complex feature interactions, enhancing the
model’s dynamic processing capability and accuracy. The method was validated on the Oil and Gas Gathering
and Transportation Full-Process Industrial Platform Attack-Defense Field, and the Catalytic Reforming Unit
Process Platform at the Key Laboratory of Information Security for the Petrochemical Industry in Liaoning
Province. Experimental results show that the proposed EfficientTransformer improves accuracy by 1.01%
and 2.26% compared to the standard Transformer on the two datasets and significantly reduces testing time,
demonstrating its applicability in the field of industrial information security.
 INDEX TERMS Intrusion detection, industrial control network, transformer, 1D-CNN, feature extraction.
 I. INTRODUCTION
 ICS play a crucial role in modern industries, particularly
in sectors like energy production, petrochemicals, and steel
manufacturing. These systems automate production pro-
cesses, improving efficiency and safety. However, traditional
ICS designs primarily focus on functional safety through
physical isolation, often neglecting network security. While
this approach may protect against some basic threats, the
increasing frequency of cyberattacks has highlighted the
vulnerability of ICS, especially in critical sectors like
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Brian Ng .
healthcare, government, and education, which have become
prime targets for hackers.
According to IT Governance’s 2024 report, the frequency
and impact of global cyberattacks are rising rapidly. In the
first half of 2024 alone, there was an average of 1,636 cyber-
attacks per week worldwide, representing a 30% increase
compared to the previous year. This trend underscores the
growing security risks faced by ICS, which require more
advanced protective measures [1].
Although traditional IDS are widely used in ICS envi-
ronments, they have several limitations. First, rule-based
IDS depend on predefined attack signatures, making them
ineffective against unknown or mutated threats. Second, these
 VOLUME 13, 2025 2025 The Authors. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License. For more information, see https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ 37931\n\n---\n\n## Page 128\n\nJ. Liu et al.: EfficientTransformer: A Dynamic Anomaly Detection Model for Industrial Control Networks
 systems often generate a high volume of false positives
and negatives, affecting the accuracy of detection [2].
Lastly, maintaining and updating the rule libraries requires
significant human effort, leading to increased operational
costs.
In recent years, deep learning techniques have emerged as
a promising solution for intrusion detection in network traffic.
These models can automatically learn features and recognize
patterns effectively, but their high computational demands
pose a significant challenge in industrial environments with
limited resources. Additionally, feature redundancy and
complex interactions further burden deep learning models,
reducing system efficiency.
To address these challenges, this paper proposes a dynamic
anomaly detection model based on EfficientTransformer.
The model integrates 1D-CNN and a linear multi-head self-
attention mechanism, enabling the retention of both local
and global information while effectively reducing feature
redundancy and computational complexity. This approach is
particularly suited for handling complex industrial protocols,
dynamic data streams, and a variety of threats.
 II. RELATED WORK
 In the field of industrial network security, deep learning has
become a mainstream approach, especially methods such
as CNN. Song et al. [3] proposed the CSK-CNN model,
which used CNN to experiment on the UNSW-NB15 and
CICIDS2017 datasets, achieving accuracy rates of 98.87%
and 99.81%, respectively. With further research, CNN has
also been applied to sequence data. Chen Hong et al. [4]
proposed a module integrating 1D-CNN and multi-layer
BiLSTM, and experimental results showed that the model had
high accuracy and recall on the NSL-KDD and CICIDS2017
datasets. Nguyen and Kim [5] proposed a CNN model based
on a genetic algorithm, which first used a genetic algorithm
combined with KNN fitness functions and fuzzy C-means
clustering for feature selection, obtaining an improved feature
subset.
Gautam et al. [6] proposed a deep learning method
based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated
Recurrent Units (GRU), called Bi-directional Recurrent
Neural Networks (Bi-RNN). This method achieved 99.13%
classification accuracy on the CICIDS2017 dataset. Srini-
vas et al. [7] used an SFDO-based deep RNN and achieved
96.14% accuracy on the BoT-IoT dataset. Donkol et al. [8]
proposed an Enhanced Long Short-Term Memory (ELSTM)
technique, combining RNN (ELSTM-RNN) to enhance the
security of IDS. Wu et al. [9] proposed a real-time deep
anomaly detection framework, specifically for multivariate
time-series data in industrial IoT. This framework, based
on CNN and two-stage LSTM autoencoders (AE), can
detect anomalies and rare events in massive sensor data
in real time. Experimental results showed that the model
not only outperforms others in performance but can also
be optimized and quantized to run on resource-constrained
edge devices, making it suitable for real-time monitoring
in industrial environments. Laghrissi et al. [10] proposed a
machine learning-based anomaly detection method focused
on communication networks in ICS. This method used
1D CNN, LSTM, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and
Isolation Forest (iForest) algorithms for anomaly detection.
Experimental results showed that the 1D CNN model
demonstrated excellent performance with 92% accuracy and
91% F1 score on the CICIDS2017 dataset, highlighting the
potential of machine learning technologies in ICS security.
In the domain of dynamic behavior detection, models
based on Graph Neural Networks (GNN) have achieved
significant results. For instance, King et al. [11] proposed
EdgeTorrent, an end-to-end anomaly-based intrusion detec-
tion method for source flow graph analysis. The method
leverages high-performance Message Passing Neural Net-
works (MPNN) to embed temporal and topological changes
in the graph, and an adversarial-trained sequence analyzer to
detect anomalous behaviors. EdgeTorrent achieved real-time
inference on graphs containing over a billion edges and
was the first to fully classify the StreamSpot dataset,
demonstrating excellent performance on real-world datasets.
Additionally, in the unsupervised network IDS field,
Lanvin et al. [12] proposed AE-pvalues, a posterior expla-
nation method based on autoencoder reconstruction errors
aimed at improving the interpretability of anomaly detection.
This method helps identify key network traffic features asso-
ciated with detected anomalies, assisting security analysts in
understanding the root cause of network attacks.
Transformers, by incorporating the entire sequence infor-
mation into computation, can perform parallel learning
on sequences and handle long-range dependencies more
effectively. Hu and Li [13] utilized the multi-head attention
mechanism provided by Transformer to encode and compress
temporal features of network intrusion behaviors and used a
decoder to predict the legitimacy of the tested domain names.
Li et al. [14] proposed a new network intrusion detection
method based on Transformer’s extreme semi-supervised
framework (ESeT). This framework achieved superior
detection performance by using only a small amount of
labeled data. Experimental results showed that this method
outperforms RNN and CNN.
In traditional Transformer architectures, the multi-head
self-attention mechanism computes global information for
all features in the sequence. Although it captures long-
distance dependencies, the lack of redundancy filtering
leads to high computational complexity. In high-dimensional
feature spaces, Transformers are highly sensitive to redundant
features, which ultimately impacts the overall efficiency of
the model.
In the past year, researchers have attempted to reduce
the computational burden of Transformer models. Liu et al.
[15] proposed the Swin-Transformer, which uses a shifting
window scheme to limit self-attention computations to
nonoverlapping local windows while allowing cross-window
connections to improve efficiency. However, this method
 37932 VOLUME 13, 2025\n\n---\n\n## Page 129\n\nJ. Liu et al.: EfficientTransformer: A Dynamic Anomaly Detection Model for Industrial Control Networks
 does not improve the most crucial component, the multi-
head self-attention mechanism, so the computation remains
overly complex. The combination of CNN and multi-head
self-attention mechanisms has been extensively optimized for
computer vision problems. For example, Carion et al. [16]
proposed a new object detection method that views object
detection as a direct set prediction problem, simplifying the
detection process by eliminating manually designed com-
ponents such as non-max suppression or anchor generation.
Li et al. [17] validated the importance of local mechanisms
and successfully applied them to four types of visual Trans-
formers. In the ImageNet2012 classification task, Transform-
ers with enhanced locality outperformed baseline models,
with parameter numbers and computational burdens remain-
ing almost the same. Shang et al. [18] proposed an efficient
anomaly detection method for ICS: the Deep Convolutional
Autoencoding Transformer Network (CAE-T). This method
extracts spatial features through convolutional autoencoders
and combines transformer architectures to capture long-term
temporal dependencies. The experimental results showed that
CAE-T performed excellently in multiple datasets of ICS,
improving F1 scores by about 70.8% and AUC by 9.2%. This
model improved detection accuracy through optimization
functions and is suitable for real-time fault monitoring.
He et al. [19] proposed a network intrusion detection method
based on the Deformable Visual Transformer (DE-VIT).
By introducing deformable attention mechanisms, the model
selects key positions in the attention mechanism based on data
dependencies, focusing on relevant areas, capturing more
useful features, and reducing memory and computational
overhead. The experimental results showed that the model
achieved 99. 5% precision in the CIC IDS2017 dataset and
97. 5% in the UNSW-NB15 dataset, outperforming other
models in addressing data imbalance issues. Peng et al. [20]
proposed a hybrid network architecture called Conformer,
which combines convolution operations with self-attention
mechanisms to enhance representation learning ability. The
conformer uses parallel structures to maximize local feature
retention and global representation. The experimental results
showed that Conformer improved the accuracy by 2. 3% over
visual Transformers in the ImageNet dataset. However, its
design is primarily targeted at image tasks, making it less
suitable for directly handling complex sequential features and
redundant information in industrial network traffic.
Drawing inspiration from existing studies and identifying
limitations in current methods, we propose the Efficient-
Transformer model. After analyzing anomaly detection
methods based on CNN and LSTM (e.g., Chen et al. [4],
Nizam et al. [21]), we found that while these methods perform
well in certain scenarios, they still face challenges in dealing
with feature redundancy, complex feature interactions, and
high computational burden. Specifically, while traditional
Transformer models can handle long-range dependencies,
their multi-head self-attention mechanism results in high
computational complexity, limiting real-time response capa-
bilities an important challenge identified in prior research.
Building on this, we introduced the linear multi-head self-
attention mechanism to alleviate the computational burden,
while leveraging a 1D-CNN to extract local features, leading
to the EfficientTransformer model. Compared to previous
methods, EfficientTransformer not only optimizes compu-
tational efficiency but also addresses the class imbalance
issue through a weighted cross-entropy loss function, further
enhancing the model’s anomaly detection performance. The
design of this model was inspired by the analysis and
improvements made on the real-world challenges presented
in the literature.
 III. METHODS
 Fig. 1 presents the research route of the dynamic anomaly
detection model based on the EfficientTransformer.
Step 1: To achieve dynamic network traffic analysis and
threat detection, Suricata and ELK are used to capture and
parse identifiable network traffic, represented in numerical
and textual formats. Non-numeric attributes underwent one-
hot encoding, and entries containing non-numeric values
(NaN) are removed to facilitate model processing.
Step 2: The EfficientTransformer leverages its ability to
learn both local and global features to quickly identify
abnormal patterns and potential threats. By applying feature
weighting, it addresses the issues of feature redundancy and
learning of complex feature relationships.
The EfficientTransformer Encoder contains four key
modules: 1D-CNN, Linear Multi-Head attention, layerNor-
malization [22], and positionalencoding.
The model construction route proposed in this paper is as
follows.
 A. 1D CNN
 1D CNN, a neural network architecture commonly used
for processing sequential data, employs filters or convolu-
tional kernels as small arrays of learnable weights. During
training, these weights are continuously updated using the
backpropagation algorithm. The filters slide along the input
data (typically a one-dimensional sequence), performing
element-wise multiplication with local regions of the input
data and summing the results to produce a single value
in the output. The output sequence generated by sliding
each filter over the input sequence through convolution is
referred to as a feature. Fig. 2 illustrates this process. A 1D-
CNN has stronger feature extraction capabilities because each
convolutional kernel processes all input channels, making it
more powerful in capturing complex patterns in the input
data. Through its unique local perception and shared weight
mechanisms, this local perception ability not only enhances
the model’s sensitivity to important features but also reduces
the necessity to process redundant information, thereby
lowering computational complexity.

Several commands and traffic data in industrial protocols
exhibit local dependencies. Whether it is a time-series-based
protocol such as Modbus, DNP3, or other control network
protocols, 1D-CNN can learn their local patterns through
convolutional kernels, making it highly adaptable.
 B. LINEAR MULTI-HEAD ATTENTION
 The most important aspect of the linear multi-head self-
attention mechanism is its low computational complexity
and efficient learning ability. In the traditional multi-head
self-attention mechanism, the kernel function is the Softmax
function, which results in quadratic computational complex-
ity. When the sequence is very long, computation becomes
particularly complex and inefficient. ReLU Attention reduces
this complexity significantly by replacing the Softmax
function with a linear function, thereby improving processing
speed and scalability.
