The entire computational process becomes linear.
Although the weights are no longer strictly normalized, the
relevance between the query and key can still be determined
using the dot product QK T . The higher the relevance, the
more important the generated value. A ReLU activation is
applied to transform this relevance, producing the weights
used to scale the value matrix V , where important features
are amplified and less important features are diminished, thus
achieving weighted processing.
A key advantage of the linear multi-head self-attention
mechanism is that it leverages the associative proper-
ties of matrix multiplication, reducing the computational
complexity from quadratic to linear while maintaining its
functionality. This makes linear attention more advantageous
when processing large-scale data, as it allows for more
efficient computation. Hybrid attention, by combining linear
attention with 1D convolution operations, overcomes the
limitations of linear attention in local feature extraction.
 C. LAYER NORMALIZATION
 Layer normalization provides a more flexible normalization
method by normalizing the output of each layer indepen-
dently for every sample, rather than normalizing over a batch
of data. In layer normalization, for a given sample, the mean
and variance of all activations in that layer are calculated and
used to normalize the activations, making their mean zero
and variance one. The equation for Layer Normalization is
as follows :
 LayerNorm( x ) = ε x i → μ ↑ ϑ 2 + ϖ + ϱ (9)
Where x i represents the i-th input feature value, μ is the mean
of all x i values, ϑ 2 is the variance of all x i values, ε and ϱ are
learnable scaling and shift parameters, respectively.
 D. POSITIONAL ENCODING
 Positional encoding is an important technique used to provide
the model with information regarding the position of each
element in the input sequence. Absolute positional encoding
directly adds a unique code to the elements at each position,
independent of other elements’ positions. This encoding is
generated using sine and cosine functions, which depend
on the fixed position of each element in the sequence. The
encoding for each position was precomputed and added
directly to the input embeddings, ensuring that each position
had distinct positional information.

 E. WEIGHTED CROSS-ENTROPY LOSS
 In industrial control networks, there is often a data imbalance
between normal and abnormal traffic, with abnormal traffic
typically representing only a small proportion. Standard loss
functions (such as cross-entropy loss) may cause the model
to overly favor the normal class, neglecting the detection
of minority classes. Therefore, the following improved loss
functions are proposed.
 L = → 1

Where L represents the loss function, N is the total number
of samples, w i is the class weight used to assign different
weights to normal and abnormal classes, y i is the true label
( y i = 1 if the sample belongs to the class, otherwise y i = 0),
 p i is the predicted probability for the class, 1 → y i is used
to calculate the loss for the negative class, log( p i ) is the
logarithmic probability of the predicted positive class, and
log(1 → p i ) is the logarithmic probability of the predicted
negative class.
By adjusting the class weight w i , EfficientTransformer
assigns a higher penalty weight to the abnormal class when
calculating the loss, allowing the model to focus more on the
feature learning of the minority class.

and ultra-long sequences, where it achieved the highest

 IV. REAL-TIME PACKET CAPTURE
 Real-time data acquisition is required to reduce detection
latency. Suricata was designed with multithreading capa-
bilities, allowing it to fully leverage modern multi-core
processors for high-throughput network monitoring. Elastic-
search is a distributed search and analytics engine commonly
used for large-scale data search, real-time analysis, and
visualization. Redis is an open-source key-value store known
for its exceptional speed that supports a variety of data
structures. Elasticsearch is built on Apache Lucene and is
the core component of the ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash,
Kibana) stack, often used inPlatforms like log analysis, full-
text search, and security intelligence. The Suricata framework
is shown in Fig. 5.
Suricata’s multithreaded design significantly enhances its
ability to handle large-scale network traffic. Each RX, W,
and TX thread can process traffic in parallel, alleviating
the bottleneck of single-threaded processing and increasing
the system’s throughput. By utilizing data queues between
threads (such as the Pickup Queue and Verdict Queue),
Suricata ensures efficient data transfer and analysis, pre-
venting blocking between different threads. At packet rates
between 1000-25000 pps, no packet loss was observed.
Packet loss occurred at 25000 pps, which exceeds the
typical communication traffic speed in industrial control
environments, proving that the system can handle traffic
capture tasks in high-speed traffic conditions.
In our platform, real-time traffic capture is performed
using the Suricata tool, which effectively captures traffic
data from various ICS. The testing computer’s IPC is
connected to a switch, and Suricata’s network interface is
configured to capture traffic packets from the platform and
send them to the ELK stack for storage and analysis. This
ensures that each packet is accurately timestamped, protocol-
identified, and contains other relevant features. The captured
 VOLUME 13, 2025 37937\n\n---\n\n## Page 134\n\nJ. Liu et al.: EfficientTransformer: A Dynamic Anomaly Detection Model for Industrial Control Networks
 packets are then organized and saved as CSV files using
Python scripts for further analysis. Anomalous traffic packets
are generated using specific attack tools (such as LOIC and
Metasploit) to simulate various types of network attacks,
including DoS attacks, MITM attacks, and others. During
the replay process, Suricata is used to re-inject the captured
packets into the testing computer’s IPC, simulating real
industrial network traffic. To ensure the accuracy of the
experiments, the captured traffic is distinguished from the
anomalous traffic injected by malicious tools. Through this
method, we can accurately replicate various attack scenarios
in the testing environment and evaluate the system’s response
and defense capabilities.

 To evaluate the detection performance of the proposed model

Training time: The time required for the model to
complete training from the start of learning. This reflects the
model’s training efficiency and its demand for computational
resources.
Testing time: The time required for the model to predict
new data. This reflects the model’s response speed in real-
world applications.
Response time: The difference between the timestamp of
data acquisition and the timestamp of the output results,
which is a key metric for measuring the system’s processing
capability, especially in dynamic systems.

 Based on trial and error, the network traffic data was

and abnormal traffic were replayed alternately to test the
model’s responsiveness to various situations. The model’s
accuracy and efficiency in handling dynamic data were

In the EfficientTransformer model configuration,
a 1D-CNN with a kernel size of 3 and stride of 1 was used
to extract local features. The linear multi-head self-attention
mechanism employs eight attention heads, each with 64-
dimensional Key/Query/Value vectors for global feature
learning. The positional encoding dimension is set to 128 to
ensure that sufficient positional information is retained.
To optimize the model’s learning efficiency, the learning rate
is set to 0.001, allowing for stable convergence and effective
feature extraction during training. Future experiments should
follow the same design.

against potential security threats.
 VI. CONCLUSION
 The EfficientTransformer model proposed in this study
effectively combines 1D-CNN and a linear multi-head self-
attention mechanism to reduce computational complexity
while effectively learning both local and global features,
improving the handling of imbalanced data. Experimental
results demonstrate that the model efficiently extracts key
features in dynamic data environments, avoiding interference
from redundant information, and performing excellently in
both accuracy and efficiency. Additionally, the model excels
when dealing with both public and non-public protocols,
maintaining an accuracy rate above 98% and showing stable
performance and reliability even after extended training.
However, while the model performs well in the current
experiments, which are based on synthetic or small-scale
datasets, there are limitations in its adaptability to more com-
plex, real-world industrial control environments. Synthetic
datasets may not fully reflect the diverse range of potential
threats in industrial control systems, potentially leaving
out certain types of attacks. Therefore, future work will
incorporate more diverse datasets, particularly those from
different industrial sectors, to comprehensively assess the
model’s generalizability in a variety of real-world scenarios.
Moreover, we plan to further enhance the model by
integrating cross-modal attention mechanisms to improve
its precision and flexibility, particularly in the context of
multimodal data fusion. This will allow the model to
dynamically adjust feature weights based on the current
environment, enabling more effective detection of complex
attacks and improving its overall detection capability in
industrial control networks.
Future research will also focus on evaluating the model’s
performance on more diverse and imbalanced datasets,
as well as comparing it to other state-of-the-art models
optimized for industrial control system anomaly detection.
By addressing the limitations of synthetic or small-scale
datasets and enhancing the model’s adaptability and response
to real-world attacks, we aim to advance the development
of intrusion detection technologies for industrial control
networks, providing more robust and efficient solutions for
practical applications.

 ABSTRACT Industrial Control Systems (ICS) are critical to the efficient operation of essential sectors such
as manufacturing, energy, and water management. However, their increasing integration with IT systems
exposes them to sophisticated cyberattacks, particularly lateral attacks targeting Programmable Logic
Controllers (PLCs). Advanced preventive measures are necessary because, despite their significance, many
ICS continue to rely on outdated technologies with few security features. This paper proposes a machine
learning (ML)-based approach to anomaly detection in ICS communication networks, focusing on techniques
such as 1D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Support
Vector Machines (SVMs), and Isolation Forest (iForest) algorithms. We generated a dataset by capturing both
normal and manipulated ICS communication patterns, including TCP/IP traffic. Simulated lateral attacks
provided realistic data for training and testing the ML models. The results demonstrate that the 1D CNN
model achieved the highest accuracy (0.92) and F1 score (0.91) with minimal processing time, making it
ideal for real-time intrusion detection. This research highlights the potential of ML techniques to fortify ICS
cybersecurity and lays the groundwork for future advancements in critical infrastructure resilience.
 INDEX TERMS Anomaly detection, intrusion detection systems, machine learning, threat detection,
programmable logic controllers.
 I. INTRODUCTION
 Industrial control systems (ICS) form the backbone of critical
infrastructures across multiple sectors. Traditionally iso-
lated, these systems are now increasingly interconnected,
exposing them to cyber threats that exploit outdated pro-
tocols and hardware. Despite the critical nature of ICS,
existing cybersecurity solutions often lack the sophistica-
tion required to address modern threats. Machine Learning
(ML) techniques provide a promising approach for detecting
these threats through advanced anomaly detection systems,
enabling real-time identification of intrusions and irregulari-
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Bang L. H. Nguyen .
ties. This paper explores ML-based methods to address this
challenge, focusing on their application to programmable
logic controllers (PLCs).
The use of ML algorithms allows for the development
of robust intrusion detection systems (IDS) that can iden-
tify anomalous behaviour and potential security breaches in
real time. One approach is to, leverage the power of the
iForest, a machine-learning algorithm that excels at anomaly
detection by isolating normal instances from outliers [1].
Another method involves employing SVMs, a popular super-
vised learning algorithm known for its ability to handle
high-dimensional data and imbalanced sample sets [2], [3].
Additionally, 1D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have
proven effective in various domains and can capture complex

Benka et al.: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Anomalies, Intrusions, and Threats in ICS
 patterns in sequential data, making them suitable for detecting
anomalies in industrial control systems [4].
The aim of this paper is to explore the applicability and
effectiveness of these ML methods, including isolated forest,
support vector machine, and 1D CNNs, for threat detec-
tion, intrusion identification, and anomaly detection in ICS.
By utilizing simulated training data divided into packets and
labelled with classes (normal and modified), the paper aims
to provide insights into the performance and accuracy of
these methods. The findings of this research are expected to
contribute to the development of robust security measures
for industrial control systems, enhancing the protection of
critical infrastructures against cyber threats and ensuring the
reliability and safety of their operations.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section II provides the theoretical background, including
an overview of PLC vulnerabilities and prior work on ICS
anomaly detection. Section III describes the methodology,
including the attack simulation and data collection process.
The results of the experiments are presented in Section IV,
followed by a discussion of their implications in Section V.
 II. THEORETICAL BACKGROUND
 ICS and their components, particularly PLC’s have under-
gone significant advancements to support industrial automa-
tion. However, their increasing integration with modern IT
systems has exposed them to new vulnerabilities. This section
explores the role of PLCs in industrial automation, highlights
their vulnerabilities, and reviews existing research in anomaly
detection for ICS.
 A. PLCs IN THE IT INFRASTRUCTURE
 PLCs are fundamental to ICS, serving as controllers that exe-
cute automated processes based on pre-programmed instruc-
tions. They are essential for enabling production flexibility,
improving efficiency, and ensuring reliability in industrial
operations. Recent trends in PLC development have focused
on:
 • Scalability and Diagnostics: Enhancing the ability to
monitor and control complex industrial processes.
 • IoT Integration: Connecting devices and sensors to
support seamless communication and predictive main-
tenance.
 • Cloud Connectivity: Enabling remote access to data and
control mechanisms, improving operational visibility.
 • Virtual Commissioning: Simulating and testing control
programs before deployment to reduce risks and down-
time [5].
Despite their pivotal role, the global PLC market faces sig-
nificant security challenges. For example, the absence of
robust encryption or authentication mechanisms in legacy
PLC systems has led to an increased risk of cyberattacks.
As the market is projected to grow to USD 18.3 billion by
2030, securing these systems has become a critical priority.
The impact of the control systems and industrial automation
is huge. The market was estimated at ca 170 billion USD
(2022) and the expectations in 2023 are reaching 188 billion
USD [6].
The global PLC market was valued at USD 11,6 Bn in
2021 and the projected value in next years, e.g., the projection
in USD 18.3 Bn by 2030 [7].
Projected size of the global programmable logic controller
(PLC) market between 2020 and 2026: (in billion U.S. dol-
lars) [8], shown in Fig.1.
 FIGURE 1. Market size - PLC [8].
 For a better illustration of the PLC market, the com-

 B. CYBERSECURITY AND THREAT LANDSCAPE
 In a rapidly evolving security landscape of Europe and
beyond, the need for innovative solutions and cooper-
ation is necessary. The growing presence of renewable
energy resources, physical electric infrastructure, smart grids,
and Industry 4.0 technologies, including control systems,
SCADA, or billions of IoT devices, introduces new security
challenges. Cyberattacks on critical energy infrastructure can
have significant economic consequences, as seen in the case
of the U.S. power grid, released by Lloyd’s of London, notes
the scenario’s impact on the U.S. economy is estimated at
more than 240 billion dollars.
Generally, critical infrastructure assets could be destroyed
or degraded by both natural and human-initiated threats.
Any disruption, whether stemming from a terrorist attack,
a natural disaster, or man-made damage is likely to create a
cascading effect on any country’s energy system that is both
complex and interconnected [15]. Symantec (also known as
Norton) observed during one year of monitoring an average
of 74 targeted attacks per day globally, of which nine attacks
(16.3% of all attacks) per day were targeted towards the
energy sector [16]. Cyber-attacks present a new category of
security threats with little expertise or experience in critical
infrastructures or in industry at all.
As mentioned by the Commissioner for Humanitarian
Aid and Crisis Management Stylianides in 2014 [24] in his
 VOLUME 13, 2025 12503\n\n---\n\n## Page 144\n\nD. Benka et al.: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Anomalies, Intrusions, and Threats in ICS
 confirmation hearing to the European Parliament, 1 Euro
invested in resilience saves 7 Euro in emergency.
Attacks on ICS can range from disabling security apparatus
to inflicting direct physical damage, as highlighted by refer-
ence [25]. The security of such systems has been a growing
concern, with instances of simple code injection proven by
researchers in references [26], [27], [28], and more intricate
attacks like Stuxnet, underscoring the urgency for advanced
protective measures [19], [29]. Siemens has been incorporat-
ing cryptographic mechanisms in newer products, such as the
S7-1500 family, to overcome detected vulnerabilities [30].
However, vulnerabilities persist, with Rockwell Automation
PLC experiencing a notable one, marked as CVE-2022-
1161, allowing undetected internal code modifications [31].
Mitsubishi PLCs are not exempt, with vulnerabilities like
CVE-2022-29831, CVE-2022-29832, and CVE-2022-29833
enabling attackers to compromise connected safety CPU
modules by accessing information from GX Works3 project
files [32].
Finding more and more vulnerabilities shows how impor-
tant it is to keep improving security to protect against many
different cyber threats. Combining new security features, reg-
ular updates, and better awareness of security is key to making
these systems stronger against cyberattacks. The combined
efforts of developers, security experts, and those in the indus-
try are vital in dealing with the complex security challenges
and making these systems more reliable.
 C. PLC VULNERABILITIES
 PLCs, while critical to industrial automation, are increas-
ingly targeted by cyberattacks as they integrate with modern
IT systems. Key vulnerabilities stem from their legacy
designs, which often lack robust authentication, encryption,
and update mechanisms. For example, outdated firmware and
protocols leave PLCs susceptible to attacks such as unau-
thorized data manipulation, denial-of-service (DoS) attacks,
and lateral assaults. Addressing these vulnerabilities requires
proactive measures, including firmware updates, advanced
intrusion detection systems, and adherence to cybersecurity
best practices.
The security of PLC systems is a critical consideration,
especially in industrial and critical infrastructure settings,
where they are used to control vital operations. Common
types of vulnerabilities associated with PLCs:
 • Outdated Hardware and Software: Many PLCs lack
updates against known vulnerabilities, leaving them sus-
ceptible to exploits [9].
 • Weak Authentication and Access Control: Insufficient
mechanisms allow unauthorized users to modify PLC
configurations or commands [10].
 • Lack of Encryption: Unencrypted communication chan-
nels expose data to interception and manipulation [11].
 • Susceptibility to Malware and Ransomware: Attacks
such as Triton and Stuxnet have demonstrated the capa-
bility to disrupt PLC operations, causing significant
physical and financial damage [12], [13].
These vulnerabilities pose risks not only to industrial pro-
cesses but also to critical infrastructure sectors like energy,
water, and transportation.
To enhance the security of PLC systems, measures such as
firmware updates, strong authentication and access control,
data communication encryption, network monitoring, and
threat detection are crucial. Industrial organizations should
also follow best practices for cybersecurity and have incident
response plans in place in case of an attack. Ensuring the
security of PLC systems is a critical aspect of industrial
automation and process control [14].
 D. MACHINE LEARNING ALGORITHMS
 iForest is a type of unsupervised ML method used to discover
anomalies. With recursive partitioning, it isolates anoma-
lies and is useful for high-dimensional data. The technique
isolates instances that require fewer partitions than typical
instances and it has a unique ability to discover anoma-
lies [33]. Because of its effectiveness and capacity to manage
both numerical and categorical data types, iForest is a great
option for promptly spotting odd communication patterns that
could be signs of a cyberattack or other system issues.
Tasks involving anomaly detection and image processing
frequently make use of CNNs. Because CNNs can automat-
ically learn hierarchical feature representations from data,
they are a powerful tool for identifying spatial anomalies
in intricate industrial processes. Convolutional filters are
applied to the input data by CNNs, which helps to find pat-
terns or anomalies by capturing significant features at various
levels [34]. CNNs are useful for identifying abnormalities
such as abrupt changes in communication frequency or unex-
pected data flows inside the network because communication
patterns in ICS frequently have temporal-spatial correlations
that they can learn.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) of the LSTM type are
well suited for temporal anomaly detection in ICS, because
of their superior ability to handle sequential input. Because
of its memory cells’ ability to store data for extended periods
of time, LSTM networks can identify temporal dependencies
in time-series data. Through effective learning from past com-
munication sequences, LSTM can eventually detect patterns
that deviate from the norm and could point to cyber threats,
latency problems, or faults in the system [35]. Because of this,
LSTM is perfect for identifying irregularities in industrial
processes that show temporal fluctuations.
SVM is a supervised learning algorithm that is widely
used for classification and regression tasks. SVM works by
finding the optimal hyperplane that separates data points into
different classes, making it suitable for anomaly detection
in industrial control systems where classification of normal
and anomalous data is essential. SVM can effectively handle
high-dimensional data and has been shown to perform well
in identifying anomalies [36]. When the ICS’ data contains
some identified instances of both normal and anomalous
communication behaviour, SVM can be helpful. Its capacity
to draw a distinct decision boundary facilitates the detection
 12504 VOLUME 13, 2025\n\n---\n\n## Page 145\n\nD. Benka et al.: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Anomalies, Intrusions, and Threats in ICS
 of communication traffic anomalies that may indicate vulner-
abilities or assaults.
Each above-mentioned method targets a different area of
anomaly detection. CNN is good at capturing spatial patterns,
LSTM is good at focusing on temporal relationships, SVM
is good at classification, and iForest is good at handling
high-dimensional data. Using these algorithms enables thor-
ough identification of different kinds of anomalies in ICS
transmission.
Traditional IDS often rely on signature-based techniques,
which are limited in detecting novel or zero-day attacks.
In contrast, anomaly detection systems leverage ML to iden-
tify deviations from normal behavior. Recent research has
focused on the use of ML and artificial intelligence (AI) for
anomaly detection in automation environments, notably ICS
and the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). Several strategies
have been developed, each with the goal of addressing certain
issues inherent in these systems, including real-time process-
ing, high accuracy, and adaptation to unexpected threats.
However, it is important to note that some tools, like Snort,
primarily represent the signature-based detection paradigm,
despite the existence of third-party add-ons that incorporate
AI/ML components. Snort, developed by Cisco Systems,
is one of the most widely used open-source intrusion
detection and prevention systems (IDS/IPS/IDPS) in the
world [37]. It can be run in one of three modes: packet sniffer
mode, packet logger mode, and network intrusion detection
and prevention system mode. While some ML preprocessors
can be integrated into Snort, these are mostly third-party
additions and are not native features of the system. Thus,
Snort remains fundamentally a signature-based IDS.
The effectiveness and applicability of various IDS have
been analysed extensively in literature. In Table 1 below,
we summarize key studies on IDS tools, including their objec-
tives, metrics, strengths, and limitations.
Traditional IDS rely heavily on signature-based tech-
niques, which are successful against known threats but have
limited ability to detect novel or zero-day assaults. Anomaly
detection systems that use ML offer a considerable advan-
tage by spotting deviations from regular behavioral patterns.
Recent breakthroughs have investigated the use of ML and
AI for anomaly detection in automation environments such
as ICS and the IIoT. These initiatives are intended to address
intrinsic issues such as real-time processing, high precision,
and adaptability to unexpected threats.
Snort, among classic IDS technologies, is a prominent
example of the signature-based detection paradigm. Snort,
developed by Cisco Systems, is extensively used for its
functionality and substantial community support. It operates
in three modes: packet sniffer, packet logger, and network
intrusion detection/prevention system, allowing for flexible
deployment options. However, its reliance on predetermined
signatures limits its usefulness against new threats. While
AI/ML preprocessors can be added to Snort via third-party
add-ons, these functionalities are not native, hence Snort
remains primarily a signature-based IDS.
 TABLE 1. Comparative analysis of Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS).
 The above Table 1 provides a comparison of IDS tools,
highlighting their objectives, capabilities, and limitations.
Snort, Zeek, and Suricata are evaluated using parameters
such as detection accuracy, processing speed, scalability, and
flexibility. Snort’s signature-based method remains a draw-
back, despite its ease of usage and widespread acceptance.
Zeek excels at delivering detailed network analysis, although
it can be unnecessarily complicated for basic requirements.
Suricata’s multi-threaded architecture makes it exceptionally
efficient at managing enormous traffic volumes, but it is
resource-intensive, causing issues in large-scale implemen-
tations.
To address the limitations of classical IDS, researchers
have increasingly concentrated on machine learning-based
anomaly detection systems. Studies such as those in [38]
and [39] emphasize the shift to data-centric anomaly detec-
tion, meaning the importance of data quality and feature
engineering in strengthening cyber resilience. Reference [38]
compares supervised and unsupervised ML techniques for
anomaly detection, focusing on the challenges of feature
extraction and selection in the heterogeneous ICS context.
Behavioral intrusion detection, as discussed in [1], empha-
sizes the need of strong feature selection and ICS-specific
metrics. This study categorizes existing techniques and
identifies flaws such as the absence of adaptive learning
mechanisms that can change with dynamic ICS operations.
Reference [20] dives into the complexity of installing ML
detectors in big industrial facilities, emphasizing the impor-
tance of scalable, real-time learning models for efficiently
processing changing data streams.
Hybrid detection methods that integrate statistical and
machine learning methodologies are described in [2] and [4].
Reference [2] describes a two-stage model that combines
ARIMA for time-series forecasting and one-class SVM for
anomaly detection, improving detection accuracy. Similarly,
[4] presents a system that combines 1D CNN, autoencoders,

 and PCA to reduce false positives while increasing detection
precision in ICS.
Deep learning models, such as CNNs and LSTMs, have
shown particularly promising results when dealing with
complex ICS data. References [42] through [44] show the
potential of hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures for anomaly
detection, with good accuracy in benchmarks such as
CICIDS2017. These models accurately capture spatial and
temporal patterns in ICS data. Furthermore, as indicated
in [45], iForest has demonstrated potential in anomaly detec-
tion tasks, particularly in cases when labeled data is limited.
To enhance or supplement these prior attempts, we intro-

detection that was not covered by the earlier publications.

 E. MOTIVATION
 The integration of ICS with contemporary IT networks has
significantly increased the need for sophisticated security
measures to protect critical infrastructure. PLCs and other
ICS components are indispensable for industrial operations,
but their inherent vulnerabilities make them prime targets
for cyberattacks. Such attacks can have catastrophic conse-
quences, as demonstrated by notable incidents over the past
decade.
In 2014, a cyber-attack targeted energy companies,
infecting 250 organizations across the USA and Western
Europe [17]. The following year, a major attack on elec-
tricity operators in Ukraine disconnected 30 substations,
leaving eight provinces without electricity for several hours.
This incident impacted more than 200,000 people and
caused physical damage to ICS infrastructure [18]. Similarly,
in 2016, another cyber-attack on Kyiv’s power grid caused
widespread outages and revealed the use of malware specifi-
cally designed to compromise ICS and SCADA systems [19].
The 2017 Triton malware attack on a petrochemical plant
in Saudi Arabia further illustrated the destructive poten-
tial of ICS-targeted cyber threats. By crippling the plant’s
safety systems, this attack underscored how adversaries could
directly endanger human lives [20]. In 2019, an unnamed
virus partially shut down the factory operations of the eye-
glass lens manufacturer Hoya in Thailand, causing significant
operational disruptions [10].
More recently, the ransomware attack on Colonial Pipeline
in 2021 disrupted the fuel supply across the Eastern United
States, leading to widespread fuel shortages and economic
ramifications [21]. In 2022, a cyberattack on the wind tur-
bine manufacturer Nordex SE in Germany disabled remote
access to wind turbines, severely affecting their operation and
maintenance capabilities [22]. Finally, in 2023, a ransomware
attack on ABB, a global leader in industrial automation,
highlighted the ongoing vulnerabilities in critical industrial
infrastructure [23].
These incidents collectively demonstrate how adversaries
exploit vulnerabilities in ICS to inflict financial, operational,
and physical harm. A particularly concerning attack vec-
tor is lateral movement within networks, where intrusions
spread by exploiting flaws in protocols like TCP/IP and
UDP. Such attacks frequently bypass conventional perime-
ter defenses and pose a significant threat to the integrity
of industrial systems. Addressing these challenges requires
advanced anomaly detection mechanisms capable of identi-
fying unusual communication patterns that signal potential
threats.
Machine learning (ML) provides a promising solution for
this critical issue by enabling real-time monitoring and adap-
tive anomaly detection in ICS communications. This study
evaluates the effectiveness of various ML models, including
Isolation Forest (iForest), Support Vector Machines (SVMs),
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and 1D Convo-
lutional Neural Networks (CNNs). These models are assessed
to determine their suitability for detecting sophisticated lat-
eral attacks and ensuring the security of ICS networks.
 III. METHODOLOGY
 In this section, the proposed ML anomaly detection algo-
rithms are described, followed by a description of data
collection from industrial network.
The methodology consists of several stages: problem iden-
tification, attack mitigation strategy, algorithm selection, data
collection, and experimental setup. Each stage is designed
to ensure comprehensive evaluation and effective anomaly
detection.
 A. PROBLEM IDENTIFICATION
 First, we identify the types of attacks that may occur on the
ICS and the common ways to mitigate them. Lateral attacks
pose a unique challenge within ICS networks due to their
 12506 VOLUME 13, 2025\n\n---\n\n## Page 147\n\nD. Benka et al.: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Anomalies, Intrusions, and Threats in ICS
 ability to mimic normal communication patterns. This paper
identifies key types of anomalies indicative of such attacks:
 • Unauthorized Data Manipulation: Injection of rogue
commands or altered data packets.
 • Communication Floods: Overwhelming devices with
excessive traffic.
 • Protocol Exploitation: Misuse of TCP/IP or UDP proto-
cols to gain unauthorized access.
The primary objective is to detect these anomalies by analyz-
ing communication patterns between PLCs.
 B. ATTACK MITIGATION STRATEGY
 The chosen approach to mitigate lateral attacks is through
anomaly detection, where anomalous communication pat-
terns are identified as potential security threats. Anomaly
detection is a critical process across many disciplines, allow-
ing for the discovery of unusual occurrences or behaviors.
By learning patterns from large datasets and successfully
detecting abnormalities, ML approaches have emerged as
strong tools for automating anomaly identification.
The approach emphasizes:
 • Pattern Recognition: Detecting irregularities in com-
munication frequency, packet structure, or data pay-
loads.
 • Real-Time Processing: Ensuring anomalies are identi-
fied promptly to minimize operational disruptions.
 C. ALGORITHM SELECTION
 We selected several ML techniques based on their perfor-
mance in existing studies for ICS anomaly detection. The
algorithms considered include the iForest, CNNs, SVMs, and
LSTM networks. The iForest is a tree-based anomaly detec-
tion approach that builds an ensemble of random decision
trees. Because of their shorter average path lengths inside the
tree structure, each tree separates cases that are likely to be
anomalies. iForest has proven to be successful in detecting
abnormalities in ICS datasets [1].
CNNs, which are well-known for their performance in
image and signal processing applications, have also been
used in ICS anomaly detection. CNNs can discover aberrant
activities by evaluating time-series sensor data or photos
taken within the ICS environment and extracting spatial and
temporal patterns. The use of CNNs in ICS anomaly detection
has yielded encouraging results [40].
SVMs have been widely employed in anomaly detection
due to their ability to capture complicated decision bound-
aries. SVMs may be used in ICS to identify cases as normal or
abnormal based on extracted characteristics. In ICS anomaly
detection research, SVMs have proven their adaptability and
performance [41].
LSTM networks are a form of RNNs developed to solve
the vanishing gradient problem and capture long-term rela-
tionships in sequential data. LSTM networks, unlike standard
RNNs, include neurons that can store information for long
periods of time, allowing them to retain and transmit useful
information while filtering out unnecessary or duplicate
information. LSTM networks have also been used as a deep
learning approach in the context of ICS intrusion detection
to improve the accuracy and efficacy of IDS. These solutions
are designed to detect and prevent security breaches or hostile
activity in industrial networks.

The switch was configured to clone packets to port 5,
to which the Simatic field PG was connected. A simple
packet sniffer was running on the PG, storing captured data
into separate files. Physical connection was realized using

we used Simatic Manager and its NetPro tool, where the
communication was set as shown in Table 3

 E. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
 To collect data, packet sniffing was carried out in three dis-
tinct instances:
 VOLUME 13, 2025 12507\n\n---\n\n## Page 148\n\nD. Benka et al.: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Anomalies, Intrusions, and Threats in ICS
 FIGURE 3. Structure text diagram used instructions.
 • During the foundational communication among the con-
figured PLCs.
 • Basic communication between the configured PLCs
occurred with Simatic Manager set to ‘‘Online,’’ allow-
ing for the reading of the actual state from the PLCs.
 • While uploading the program (with an altered DB)
amidst the pre-configured communication among the
PLCs.
An example of structure of the PLC connection with used
instructions is shown in Figure 3.
Two networks were made for the PLC structure using the
‘‘GET’’ and ‘‘PUT’’ instructions for the PLCs to commu-
nicate with one another. In an ICS, these instructions are
essential for data exchange, guaranteeing effective and seam-
less communication between linked equipment.
Data is be read from a PLC or its partner PLC using the
‘‘GET’’ instruction, which is shown in Network 2. The REQ
input, which must be set to true to start the procedure, is what
triggers the instruction. The ID parameter establishes the
communication path and identifies the connection. The signal
NDR indicates that new data is ready after a successful data
transfer, while the ERROR and STATUS outputs reveal any
circumstances or problems that occurred during execution.
The ADDR_1 parameter, which indicates where the source
data is in the remote device, and the RD_1 parameter, which
establishes the local memory address where the received data
is placed, define the data transfer itself.
In Network 2, the ‘‘PUT’’ instruction is used to write
data to a partnering PLC. The process is started when the
REQ input is triggered, same as the GET operation. The data
is correctly routed to the intended communication channel
thanks to the connection ID. The DONE signal verifies the
data transmission once the PUT operation is successful, while
the ERROR and STATUS outputs offer diagnostics if there
are communication problems. ADDR_1 and RD_1 define the
data source and destination addresses, which guarantee that
the sent values are correctly placed in the local and distant
memory areas.
The communication process is largely controlled by the
ports and parameters that are utilized in both networks,
including REQ, ID, NDR, DONE, ERROR, and STATUS.
These parameters ensure the system’s robustness and depend-
ability by starting and finishing the processes as well as
providing the required diagnostic data. When working in
complex network environments, the system can differenti-
ate between several channels thanks to the connection IDs
(W#16#1 for GET and W#16#3 for PUT), which uniquely
identify the communication paths.
The addresses that ADDR_1 and RD_1 specify are essen-
tial for figuring out precisely where data is to be read or stored
in the PLC’s memory. As an illustration of a clear and effi-
cient data transmission, the given structure uses DB10.DBD0
as both the source and destination address.
For industrial applications that demand quick updates
and reactions, this structure makes it possible for PLCs to
communicate in real time. In order to facilitate speedy diag-
nostics, it also includes error handling methods. ERROR and
STATUS outputs promptly signal communication failures or
irregularities. By enabling targeted data transfers to memory
blocks, the GET and PUT instructions provide flexibility, and
their well-defined input and output ports make it easier to
integrate them into pre-existing PLC applications.
 F. ATTACK SCENARIOS
 An operating ICS environment with regular instructions
being sent between PLCs was used to record normal traf-
fic. On the other hand, malicious or unusual traffic was
purposefully added to produce a varied dataset for model
training. For the anomalous traffic, packets were intention-
ally modified to simulate realistic intrusion attempts. Attack
scripts introduced the following anomalies in packet contents
and structure: altered IP headers, manipulated payload con-
tents, and inserted commands to simulate unauthorized access
attempts. The ML models were able to learn and identify the
distinctions between potentially harmful and benign traffic
patterns thanks to this setup
To evaluate the proposed ML-based anomaly detection sys-
tem, a series of realistic attack scenarios were designed and
implemented. These scenarios simulate common vulnerabil-
ities and exploits within ICS, focusing on attacks targeting
PLCs through lateral communication channels.
Simulating and testing various attack scenarios in ICS
environments is essential for thorough anomaly detection
and intrusion analysis. Both malicious and benign packet
transmissions over TCP protocols were included in the attack
scenarios, which covered both standard PLC traffic flows
and altered patterns intended to resemble possible real-world
attack traffic. We simulated common attacks including packet
replay attacks, unauthorized data modification, and command
injection.
 12508 VOLUME 13, 2025\n\n---\n\n## Page 149\n\nD. Benka et al.: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Anomalies, Intrusions, and Threats in ICS
 The dataset was generated using a simulated PLC envi-
ronment with four independent PLCs communicating over
a managed network switch. The data collection process
included the following steps:
 • Baseline Traffic: Normal communication traffic was
captured during standard PLC operations.
 • Simulated Attack Traffic: Anomalous traffic was intro-
duced by :
 → Injecting rogue TCP/IP packets.
 → Modifying data payloads to simulate unauthorized
commands.
 → Creating communication floods to disrupt normal
operations.
Because of its reputation for dependability, TCP was selected
for attacks like data manipulation and unauthorized command
injection that call for extended connections. The attackers
sent rogue packets with altered instructions after establishing
a three-way handshake. To ensure the dataset was balanced,
approximately 70% of the traffic was normal, and 30%
consisted of attack scenarios. Packet metadata, protocol infor-
mation, and payload content were recorded for analysis.
Certain IP packet characteristics were altered to mimic hos-
tile attacks to increase the dataset’s realism. IP addresses
of source and destination nodes were changed to imitate
attackers trying to get around access control or authentication.
This technique is known as source and destination spoof-
ing. Payload modification was used to simulate unauthorized
or altered commands included in data payloads. To mimic
man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks, in which packets are
intercepted and changed before they reach their destination,
some IP header fields, including the time-to-live (TTL) and
sequence numbers, were changed. We were able to produce
increasingly complex and realistic assault scenarios through
these changes, which qualified the dataset for use in training
and testing machine learning models for intrusion detection.
 G. DATA COLLECTION SETUP
 Both raw hexadecimal and binary forms of the payload
instructions and metadata (such as source and destination IP
addresses, ports, and timestamps) were included in the packet
captures. This thorough gathering made sure that the dataset
was balanced between attack and regular data and indicative
of different forms of traffic.
GET and PUT blocks built into the PLCs’ firmware, set
as stated in Table 4, helped PLCs communicate with one
another.
 TABLE 4. Communication GET/PUT blocks.
 Data packets related to communication were mirrored by
the network switch to the fifth port, where a sniffer was
installed in the PG/PC station to capture the packets. These
packets were then stored in hexadecimal format as raw data,
which were subsequently used to create the ML model’s
training dataset.
The 70-30 ratio of data division allowed us to keep the
balance between the classifications quite well. This is signif-
icant because a model may perform well by just predicting
the majority category in a highly imbalanced dataset, which
could lead to deceptive accuracy estimates. We also used
metrics like precision, recall, and F1-score to evaluate model
performance more accurately to address this problem.
Most of the anomalous traffic comprised of simulated
lateral attacks, which were meant to imitate realistic attack
vectors. These included illegal data access and manipula-
tion between PLCs. The attacks were created by combining
replay assaults — in which malicious behaviour was added
to previously recorded regular traffic—with carefully con-
structed attack scripts that attempt to take over PLCs without
authorization or insert fake data. This method made sure that
both covert and overt intrusion attempts were recorded in the
dataset.
The sniffer used for data acquisition was written in C#
using the SharpPcap library, which allows for efficient packet
capture. After initializing a list of active devices, it asks the
user to choose an adapter from the list of choices. It config-
ures a FileStream to write the captured packets to a designated
file upon user selection; it handles file capacity limitations by
generating additional files as needed. Error handling made
sure that data capture remained reliable even when wrong
inputs were present.
To ensure thorough data collecting for this paper, the sniffer
recorded all data sent over the network, without any filters.
The key features that were retrieved and examined were:
 • Packet Metadata: Each packet contains its source and
destination IP addresses, ports, and timestamps, giving
a comprehensive picture of the communication flows
between devices.
 • Protocol Information: Data about protocols (e.g. TCP
and UDP) to examine the many kinds of network con-
nections.
 • Payload Content: Each packet contains raw data that
provides insight into the real data that is transmitted
between PLCs and other network devices.
 • Traffic Volume and Timing: Analysis of patterns in net-
work usage by analysis of packet size, frequency, and
transmission timing can help spot anomalies.
These features provided a comprehensive understanding
of both typical operations and possible security risks.
We addressed the potential concerns with class imbalance
by carefully building the dataset to ensure that both regular
and attack traffic were appropriately represented. To prevent
skewing the model’s learning process toward the majority
 VOLUME 13, 2025 12509\n\n---\n\n## Page 150\n\nD. Benka et al.: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Anomalies, Intrusions, and Threats in ICS
 class (regular traffic), the dataset was specifically created to
maintain a 70:30 ratio of normal to attack traffic.
To achieve this balanced representation, we implemented
the following steps:
 • Data augmentation: To simulate a variety of lateral
attacks, including command injections, data manipula-
tion, and illegal access, we added synthetic instances to
the attack stream.
 • Stratified sampling: To improve the generalizability of
the model, we kept the class distribution constant across
the test, validation, and training sets.
 • Comprehensive metrics: In addition to accuracy, the
model’s ability to identify anomalies was verified using
precision, recall, F1-score.
The dataset consists of 10000 packets, with a balanced distri-
bution of 70% normal traffic and 30% anomalous traffic.
The data collection process involved recording normal traf-
fic during standard PLC operations and generating anoma-
lous traffic by simulating realistic cyber-attack scenarios.
These scenarios included rogue TCP/IP packets, unautho-
rized command modifications, and communication floods,
which were designed to represent potential threats in indus-
trial control system environments.
Each packet in the dataset was captured in its raw hex-
adecimal and binary formats, providing detailed insights into
the communication patterns. Additional metadata, such as
source and destination IP addresses, timestamps, and protocol
information, was included alongside the payload. These com-
prehensive details ensure that the dataset is well-suited for
training and evaluating machine learning models in detecting
anomalies within industrial control system communications.
 H. MACHINE LEARNING ALGORITHMS
 We employed several ML algorithms. Those include a 1D
CNN, an iForest a one-class SVM, and a LSTM network.
Our paper’s ML algorithms function in a serial structure,
meaning the layers in each algorithm are connected sequen-
tially one after the other.
The data were organized into two categories, normal
and unusual communication. Normal communication means,
there are only the instructions running, and the data flow
is captured. Unusual communication means that there is a
change in the communication. This includes changes in the
instructions, connection of an unknown device etc.
The way the layers of the used algorithms are connected
in a series is shown in the figures below. Before sending its
processed output to the next layer, each algorithm operates
independently to carry out its designated task. Working in a
serial manner allows the system to fully comprehend the data
because each layer of the algorithm concentrates on a differ-
ent component of the data, improving the overall accuracy
and detection capability.

In terms of accuracy and F1 score, the 1D CNN model

training accuracy was 0.91, and the testing accuracy was 0.92,

admirably. The average processing time per file was about

The reduced processing time not only improves the system’s
responsiveness but also optimizes resource usage.

for its use in a variety of industrial contexts. Its capacity to
evaluate sequential data makes it ideal for time-series analysis
jobs such as anomaly detection in control system communi-
cations. Industries that rely on complex control systems, such

 V. CONCLUSION & DISCUSSION
 PLC vulnerabilities present a broad danger, including oper-
ational interruption, illegal access, and possible safety risks.
According to [14], ensuring the security of PLC systems is not
only an auxiliary worry, but a vital requirement in industrial
automation and process control. The greater impact of safe-
guarding these systems goes beyond individual components,
influencing the entire integrity and efficiency of industrial
operations.
The suggested solution not only addresses significant PLC
vulnerabilities, but it also helps to reduce machine down-
time, which is an important aspect in improving production
efficiency. By reducing downtime, the method enhances oper-
ational resilience and maximizes resource usage in industrial
settings. However, the actual test of the presented paradigm
is its real-world applicability. Implementing and extensively
testing this approach on genuine PLC systems will reveal crit-
ical insights into its flexibility and ability in the complexity
of real-world industrial settings.
A thorough evaluation that considers both network dynam-
ics and PLC functions will provide a more complete picture
of the model’s effectiveness. This dual assessment technique
ensures a full grasp of the model’s performance across sev-
eral operating scenarios, allowing for a strong defensive
mechanism against possible threats. Fine-tuning the model
based on ongoing input and performance measurements from
real-world deployments will be critical for increasing its
resilience and dependability. An iterative strategy based on
refinement and adaptation is critical for effectively detecting
and reducing risks in industrial control systems.
The 1D CNN’s combination of accuracy and processing
speed makes it an ideal candidate for real-time deploy-
ment in ICS environments. Its ability to detect anomalies
promptly can minimize disruptions, prevent damage, and
enhance overall system reliability. By addressing anoma-
lies in TCP/IP traffic, this framework provides a versatile
solution for protecting ICS against various lateral attack sce-
narios. The focus on simulated lateral attacks ensures that
the models are trained for real-world threats. Despite the
presence of ICS solutions on the market, the specific focus
on industrial security, particularly regarding PLCs, remains
insufficient. The proposed system aims to bridge this gap
by concentrating on industrial networks with a dedicated
emphasis on PLCs. Pursuing a specialized system tailored
to industrial security is a forward-thinking endeavour, with
the potential to significantly enhance the resilience of critical
infrastructure. Adopting ML-based anomaly detection sys-
tems can significantly strengthen the cybersecurity posture
of critical infrastructure sectors such as energy, water, and
manufacturing. This research contributes to the growing body
of knowledge required to secure these vital systems in the era
of Industry 4.0.
While ML-based models offer significant benefits for iden-
tifying threats in ICS, they also have drawbacks, such as
difficulty obtaining labelled data, vulnerability to adversar-
ial attacks, interpretability problems, resource constraints,
and adaptation to changing environments. To solve these
problems, it is critical to carefully analyse data gathering
strategies, implement model explainability approaches, main-
tain ongoing monitoring and retraining, and maybe merge
ML with traditional security measures. Striking a balance
between these parameters is essential for successful and
dependable intrusion detection in industrial settings.
In conclusion, continual validation and improvement based
on real-world insights are required to show the feasibility and
efficacy of sophisticated ML approaches for protecting ICS
from future threats. This strategy not only reduces present
risks, but also creates the groundwork for incorporating
cutting-edge technology in the continued quest of industrial
cybersecurity excellence.

 Article
 Comparative Evaluation of Temperature, Bottle Type, and
Amphotericin B on Fungal Detection in Corneal Preservation
Media Using the BACT/ALERT System ®
Aleix Fernández 1, *, Margarita Blanco 1 , Cristina Garcia 1 , Mariama Jallow 1 , Sara Monge 1 , Mar López 1 ,
Marina Hortol à 2,3 , Elba Agustí 2,3 , Anna Vilarrodona 2,3 and Gloria Soria 1,4, *
 1 Microbiology Laboratory, Banc de Sang i Teixits, 08005 Barcelona, Spain 2 Barcelona Tissue Bank, Banc de Sang i Teixits, 08005 Barcelona, Spain 3 Donació i Trasplantament d’ Ò rgans, Teixits i c è l · Lules, Vall d’Hebron Institut de Recerca (VHIR),
08035 Barcelona, Spain 4 Grup de Medicina Transfusional, Vall d’Hebron Institut de Recerca (VHIR), 08035 Barcelona, Spain
 * Correspondence: aleix.fernandez.beltran@gmail.com (A.F.); mgsoria@bst.cat (G.S.)
 Abstract
 Fungal contamination of donor corneas, although rare, constitutes a serious infection risk
to recipients. Therefore, microbiological quality control with methods optimized for fungal
detection is crucial in eye banks to detect and discard contaminated corneas. This study
aimed to compare the performance of different BACT/ALERT ® bottles (iFA Plus and
iLYM) incubated at different temperatures (32 → C and 37 → C) when corneal preservation
media, with or without amphotericin B, were cultured. A total of 6 culture conditions were
compared by inoculation of fewer than 100 colony-forming units of 18 fungi ( 10 yeasts
and 8 filamentous fungi). iFA Plus bottles incubated at 32 → C reliably detected 94.4% of
fungi, regardless of amphotericin B presence, while iLYM bottles detected 77.8% in the
absence of amphotericin B and 72.2% in its presence. At 37 → C, iFA Plus fungal detection
decreased to 61.1%. iFA Plus bottles incubated at 32 → C provided the highest detection
rates, effectively neutralizing the effect of amphotericin B and enabling recovery of both
yeasts and filamentous fungi, except for Cladosporium . Our findings support that the
optimal strategy for cornea sterility testing is incubating iFA Plus bottles at 32 → C for
optimal fungal recovery, while maintaining iFN Plus at 37 → C to allow timely detection of
anaerobic bacteria.
 Keywords: cornea; transplantation; fungal detection; BACT/ALERT ® ; iFA Plus; iLYM;
yeasts; filamentous fungi; 32 → C; 37 → C
 1. Introduction
 Corneal transplantation, or keratoplasty, is a surgical procedure that replaces damaged
or non-functional corneal tissue with healthy donor tissue. This treatment is essential
for managing various ocular conditions affecting the cornea’s shape, transparency, or
structural integrity—such as degenerative diseases, hereditary dystrophies, trauma, or
infections—making it one of the most performed transplants worldwide [ 1 ]. Different
transplantation modalities exist depending on the type and location of corneal damage.
The classical technique, penetrating keratoplasty (PK), involves replacing the full thickness
of the cornea but presents drawbacks such as structural graft failure and a higher risk
of immune rejection [ 2 ]. Recently, lamellar keratoplasties—both anterior (Deep anterior
 Microorganisms 2025 , 13 , 2562 https://doi.org/10.3390/microorganisms13112562\n\n---\n\n## Page 156\n\nMicroorganisms 2025 , 13 , 2562 2 of 17
lamellar keratoplasty-DALK) and posterior (Descemet’s stripping automated endothelial
keratoplasty-DSAEK, Descemet Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty-DMEK)—have gained
prominence by enabling selective replacement of damaged corneal layers while preserving
healthy recipient tissue, resulting in faster visual recovery and reduced rejection rates [ 3 , 4 ].
The reported incidence rates of post-keratoplasty infection differ considerably from
0.02 to 13% depending on transplant type and geographic region, with a preponderance
of bacteria over fungi and Staphylococcus spp. as the leading pathogen [ 5 – 10 ]. Fungal
infections account for less than 20% of cases and occur more often in warm and humid
environments, with Candida spp. being the most prevalent pathogen, although Fusarium
 spp. and Aspergillus spp. infections have also been reported [ 5 ]. Infection can lead to serious
complications, including graft rejection and failure. It requires antimicrobial treatment and
even surgical interventions in medically refractory cases and may result in reduced visual
acuity or even blindness of the patient [ 5 ]. Mycoses are among the most difficult corneal
transplant infections to treat [10,11].
Microbial contamination of donor tissues stands as an important factor among others
contributing to infection, such as host health status, topical corticosteroid use, suture-related
problems or previous corneal infection [ 6 ]. Although its usefulness is controversial because
there is no clear correlation to infection [ 12 ], corneoscleral rim cultures performed with
surplus tissue after surgery show contamination rates ranging from 0.37% to 14% [ 7 , 12 – 16 ],
with bacteria being more prevalent than fungi, and Staphylococcus spp. and Candida spp.
the main representatives, respectively. Some studies have shown a much higher agreement
between rim culture and fungal infections when compared with bacterial infections [ 16 , 17 ]
and propose their use to guide prophylactic treatment.
Cornea contamination may occur during procurement, handling or storage [ 9 , 18 , 19 ]
since a variety of microorganisms are present on the eyelids and conjunctival sacs of normal
eyes [ 9 ]. Different factors such as the donor’s cause of death, antibiotic use, and length
of hospital stay prior to death may influence the microbial load of the ocular surface and
increase the risk of contamination [ 20 , 21 ]. Additionally, the prevalence and microbial
spectrum vary depending on the geographic region and the specific practices of each eye
bank [18,19].
Furthermore, microbiological controls are performed at different time points during
storage and contaminated corneas are discarded. These controls have shown annual
contamination rates of corneal preservation media ranging from 1.1% to 7.2% with bacterial
contamination being the most prevalent (78% to 97% of positive cultures). Gram-Positive
bacteria, including Staphylococcus spp., Corynebacterium spp., and Bacillus spp., followed by
Gram-Negative bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa , Enterobacter spp., and Klebsiella
 spp., and fungi such as Candida spp. were the most frequent isolates [9,19–25].
Therefore, the prevention of infection resulting from microbial contamination of donor
tissues is a major challenge. Eye banks have instituted several measures, such as aseptic
techniques during corneal tissue procurement and disinfection protocols with povidone-
iodine, to try to decrease contamination of donor corneal tissue. Storage conditions are also
a critical factor. Hypothermia (2–8 → C) is the most commonly applied method of storage,
which allows storage for 7–14 days. Organ culture (28–37 → C), which extends storage time
to 4 weeks, is used widely in European eye banks [ 26 ]. Warmer temperatures are more
favorable to microbial growth, but extended storage time increases the probability to detect
contamination when cultures are routinely performed [ 9 ], which is one of the most crucial
steps for tissue stored by organ culture. This practice may contribute to the significantly
reduced rates of positive postoperative rim cultures with organ culture storage [9].
Storage solutions typically contain antibacterial agents (gentamicin and strepto-
mycin) [ 27 , 28 ]. However, nutrient-rich conditions can also support the growth of yeasts and\n\n---\n\n## Page 157\n\nMicroorganisms 2025 , 13 , 2562 3 of 17
filamentous fungi [ 29 ]. At this point, amphotericin B has emerged as a valuable additive
to preservation media [ 30 , 31 ], as it binds to ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane via
its hydrophobic domains, forming multimeric pores in the lipid bilayer that destabilize
the membrane, increase ionic permeability, disrupt cellular homeostasis, and ultimately
cause fungal cell death [ 31 – 34 ]. However, while amphotericin B is highly effective against
some yeast species like Candida albicans and Candida tropicalis , its activity is more limited
against certain filamentous fungi, such as Fusarium spp. and Scedosporium spp., as well as
some resistant non- albicans Candida strains [ 35 ], and it is dependent on the concentration
included in the media.
In summary, fungal infection after corneal transplantation is a rare, yet potentially
devastating, postoperative complication and its incidence has been growing in recent years
with the rise of lamellar keratoplasty techniques such as DSAEK and DMEK, which require
tissue processing. Eye banks have to be prepared to effectively detect fungal contamination.
At the Blood and Tissue Bank in Barcelona, cornea processing follows the guidelines
established by the Guide to the quality and safety of tissues and cells for human applica-
tion [ 36 ] regarding donor selection, procurement, storage, quality control by evaluation of
endothelial cell viability via specular microscopy and trypan blue staining, and microbi-
ological testing. Donor corneas undergo a standardized microbiological testing protocol
designed to enable early microbial detection and to ensure the safety and quality of corneal
grafts. Three different media are used sequentially for their conservation: an extraction
medium, employed from tissue retrieval until evaluation; a preservation medium, used
to maintain the tissue for up to four weeks; and a transport medium, applied to deswell
the tissue prior to transplantation. The extraction medium is incubated at 32 → C for up
to 14 days and visually inspected daily for indicators of microbiological contamination,
such as turbidity or color change due to medium acidification. Moreover, samples from
the preservation and transport media are inoculated into one iFA Plus and one iFN Plus
BACT/ALERT ® culture bottles (bioMérieux, Marcy-l’ É toile, France) and incubated at
37 → C for 14 days to detect microbial contamination using the BACT/ALERT ® 3D sys-
tem (bioMérieux, Marcy-l’ É toile, France). Endorsed by the European Pharmacopoeia (Ph.
Eur.) for sterility testing, the BACT/ALERT is a growth-based automated system that has
demonstrated sensitivity equivalent to traditional pharmacopeia methods while markedly
reducing detection times [37,38].
However, incubation at 37 → C may not optimally support the growth and detection of
certain environmental yeasts and filamentous fungi, which often proliferate more effectively
at lower temperatures, such as 32 → C [ 29 , 39 ]. This limitation was clearly demonstrated in a
recent case in which a contaminated cornea was transplanted because the system failed to
detect Aspergillus versicolor in culture bottles incubated at 37 → C [ 40 ]. Additionally, the type
of culture bottle used can significantly influence detection sensitivity; for instance, iLYM
bottles has been reported to enhance the growth of fungal contaminants [29].
Therefore, the purpose of this study was to compare two incubation temperatures
(32 → C and 37 → C) and two types of BACT/ALERT ® culture bottles (iFA Plus and iLYM)
with two types of corneal preservation media (with or without amphotericin B) using low-
level inocula (<100 CFU/mL), in accordance with Ph. Eur. [ 36 ], with the aim of determining
the optimal conditions to detect fungal contamination in corneal preservation media using
an automated system.
 2. Materials and Methods
 2.1. Fungal Strains
 A total of eighteen fungal isolates were analyzed. Sixteen were obtained from routine
microbiological controls of corneal preservation media and represented 85.7% (18 out of 21)\n\n---\n\n## Page 158\n\nMicroorganisms 2025 , 13 , 2562 4 of 17
of the fungal species identified from January 2024 until April 2025, including nine yeasts
( Candida albicans , Candida tropicalis , Candida parapsilosis , Candida glabrata , Clavispora lusita-
niae , Pichia norvegensis , Pichia kudriavzevii , Wickerhamomyces anomalus , Debaryomyces hansenii )
and seven filamentous fungi ( Aspergillus fumigatus , Penicillium chrysogenum , Arthrinium
arundinis , Cladosporium sphaerospermum , Stachybotrys chlorohalonata , Alternaria alternata , and
 Curvularia sp). All isolates were identified by Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization
Time-of-Flight (MALDI-TOF) using the MaldiBiotyper Sirius (Bruker, Bremen, Germany)
and were stored at ↑ 80 → C with 20% glycerol until use. All contaminated corneas were
discarded. Additionally, two reference fungal strains were included, prepared from com-
mercially standardized inocula (BIOBALL ® , bioMérieux, Marcy-l’ É toile, France): the yeast
 Candida albicans ATCC 10231 and the filamentous fungi Aspergillus brasiliensis ATCC 16404.
 2.2. BACT/ALERT ® System and Culture Bottles
 Microbiological monitoring was carried out using the BACT/ALERT ® 3D system
(bioMérieux, Marcy-l’ É toile, France), an automated platform that continuously monitors
culture bottles through a colorimetric sensor detecting carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) released
during microbial growth [41–43].
Two types of culture bottles were used: iFA Plus with a maximum incubation time of
14 days, and iLYM with a maximum incubation time of 7 days. The iFA Plus bottles contain
an aerobic complex medium with polymeric beads that neutralize residual antimicrobials,
supporting the growth of a broad range of aerobic and facultative microorganisms [ 44 ].
The iLYM bottles contain an acidic, carbohydrate-enriched medium designed to promote
the growth of yeasts, filamentous fungi, and some facultative anaerobes, but not strict
anaerobes [45].
 2.3. Corneal Preservation Media
 The suitability of the BACT/ALERT ® system was evaluated for six corneal media:
Corneal Chamber ® (AL.CHI.MI.A, Ponte San Nicol ò , PD, Italy) is an extraction medium
containing the Eusol-C solution and gentamicin, for corneal storage up to 14 days at 4 → C;
Kerasave ® (AL.CHI.MI.A, Ponte San Nicol ò , PD, Italy) is an extraction medium, contain-
ing the Eusol-C solution, gentamicin, streptomycin and amphotericin B at 2.5 μ g/mL, for
corneal storage up to 30 days at 4 → C; Tissue-C ® (AL.CHI.MI.A, Ponte San Nicol ò , PD,
Italy) is a preservation medium for corneal storage at 31 → C that contains penicillin G,
streptomycin and amphotericin B; Carry-C ® (AL.CHI.MI.A, Ponte San Nicol ò PD, Italy)
is a transport medium for corneal deswelling at room temperature, which also contains
penicillin G, streptomycin, amphotericin B and dextran; Cornea Max ® (Eurobio, Les Ulis,
France) is a preservation medium for corneal storage at 31 → C up to 30 days, which is sup-
plemented with amphotericin B at 0.25 μ g/mL; Cornea Jet ® (Eurobio, Les Ulis, France) is a
transport medium for corneal deswelling at room temperature, which is also supplemented
with amphotericin B at 0.25 μ g/mL.
 2.4. Sample and Control Preparation
 Frozen aliquots of fungal strains were thawed at room temperature and inoculated onto
selective solid media: yeast were streaked onto Tryptone Soy Agar (TSA), while filamentous
fungi were cultured on Sabouraud Dextrose agar (SDA). Plates were incubated at 32 → C for
yeasts and at 22 → C for filamentous fungi until colonies became macroscopically visible.
Unicellular suspensions were prepared in sterile saline, using protocols adapted to
microbial type. Yeast colonies were aseptically collected with a Kolle loop and transferred
into tubes containing sterile 0.9% NaCl. Sporulated filamentous fungi were overlaid with
sterile saline containing 0.05% Tween 20 and gently scraped with a Digralsky loop to release\n\n---\n\n## Page 159\n\nMicroorganisms 2025 , 13 , 2562 5 of 17
spores. Suspensions were allowed to settle in tubes for 15 min to remove hyphal fragments,
and the spore-enriched supernatant was transferred to new tubes for further use.
Microbial concentrations were determined using a Neubauer counting chamber and
adjusted to approximately 10 5 CFU/mL. Suspensions exceeding the target value were
diluted with sterile saline, while those below the target were reprocessed to increase the
microbial load, ensuring homogeneous suspensions at the desired concentration.
For each fungal species, a dilution series was prepared, and all subsequent inoculations
were performed in triplicate. For each replicate, 0.1 mL of a suspension containing fewer
than 100 CFU/mL was inoculated into two iFA Plus bottles and one vented iLYM bottle.
Inoculum concentrations were confirmed by plate counting.
To compare two media—Corneal Chamber and Corneal Chamber supplemented with
amphotericin B (2.5 μ g/mL)—0.9 mL of the respective medium was added per bottle, and
the procedures were carried out in parallel. One set of iFA Plus and iLYM bottles was
incubated at 32 → C, while the remaining set of iFA Plus bottles was incubated at 37 → C,
using the BACT/ALERT ® system. Positive cultures were subcultured on TSA or SDA and
identified by MALDI-TOF.
Each experiment included positive controls, in which microorganisms were inocu-
lated into bottles without corneal media, and negative controls, using sterile saline or
uncontaminated medium to verify the absence of contamination.
 2.5. Data Analysis
 Graphs and statistical analysis were performed using GraphPad Prism software ver-
sion 5.03 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA) and Microsoft Excel. Comparisons
between experimental conditions—such as bottle type and incubation temperature—were
conducted using the paired Student’s t -test. Additionally, Fisher’s exact test was applied
to assess differences in the distribution of positive and negative outcomes across these
parameters. Statistical significance is denoted in figures as: * ( p ↓ 0.05), ** ( p ↓ 0.01),
*** ( p ↓ 0.001). Non-significant differences are shown as ns ( p > 0.05), while NA denotes
cases where statistical analysis was not applicable due to absence of replicates.
 3. Results
 3.1. Previous Considerations: BACT/ALERT ® Performance
 3.1.1. Growth Promotion Properties of BACT/ALERT ® Bottles
The growth-promoting properties of each batch of culture bottles used for sterility test-
ing were routinely verified by inoculating fewer than 100 CFU of each test microorganism,
in accordance with the Ph. Eur. requirements. Aerobic iFA Plus bottles were inoculated
with Staphylococcus aureus , Pseudomonas aeruginosa , Bacillus subtilis subsp. spizizenii , Can-
dida albicans , and Aspergillus brasiliensis . Anaerobic iFN Plus bottles were inoculated with
 Clostridium sporogenes and Bacteroides fragilis . All bacterial strains were detected within
3 days and all fungal strains within 5 days, complying thus with Ph. Eur. criteria.
iLYM bottles were also evaluated for growth promotion by inoculating fewer than
100 CFU of each control strain. Under these conditions, only Pseudomonas aeruginosa and
 Candida albicans were detected by the BACT/ALERT ® system, at 27.8 and 27.5 h, respectively.
 Aspergillus brasiliensis was not detected by the system; however, post-incubation visual
inspection revealed fungal growth inside the bottles. After consulting with bioMérieux, it
was recommended to vent the bottles prior to inoculation in order to introduce oxygen and
thereby enhance fungal growth. Following this adjustment, Aspergillus brasiliensis was suc-
cessfully detected within 36 h. Consequently, vented iLYM bottles were considered suitable
for the detection of yeasts and filamentous fungi as required by Ph. Eur. requirements.\n\n---\n\n## Page 160\n\nMicroorganisms 2025 , 13 , 2562 6 of 17
3.1.2. Method Suitability
In compliance with the Ph. Eur., the suitability of the BACT/ALERT ® method for
corneal preservation media was demonstrated by evaluating specificity, sensitivity, repro-
ducibility, and robustness.
Specificity
No false-positive results were observed during the experiments. Control bottles
inoculated with uncontaminated sterile saline or corneal preservation media consistently
remained negative throughout the incubation period.
Sensitivity
The 6 corneal preservation media tested were Corneal Chamber, Kerasave, Cornea
Max, Tissue-C, Cornea Jet, and Carry-C. As the maximum volume of these media is 100 mL,
1 mL (1%) of each one was inoculated into iFA Plus BACT/ALERT ® bottles. Inocula of
<100 CFU of each test microorganism were prepared in duplicate, and time to detection
(TTD) was recorded. iFA Plus bottles were incubated at 37 → C. All microorganisms were
detected within 3 days (minimum TTD: 12.4 ± 0.1 h for Klebsiella aerogenes ; maximum
TTD: 50.3 ± 5.5 h for Aspergillus brasiliensis ), except for Cutibacterium acnes , which required
5.2 days, as shown in Figure 1. Overall, the presence of corneal media did not significantly
affect microbial detection compared with controls bottles without media.
 Figure 1. Effect of corneal preservation media on time to detection of microbial growth. Mean time to
detection (hours) with 95% confidence interval is plotted.
Effect of Inoculum
To assess the effect of inoculum size, four serial dilutions of the control strains Candida
albicans ATCC 10231 and Aspergillus brasiliensis ATCC 16404, ranging approximately from
10 4 to 10 1 CFU, were inoculated into iFA Plus bottles, and TTD was determined at 37 → C
in two independent experiments. As shown in Figure 2, TTD was inversely proportional
to inoculum size, and the system was capable of detecting as few as 1.5 CFU of Candida
albicans ATCC 10231 and 4 CFU of Aspergillus brasiliensis ATCC 16404.\n\n---\n\n## Page 161\n\nMicroorganisms 2025 , 13 , 2562 7 of 17
 Figure 2. Effect of inoculum on time to detection for ( a ) Candida albicans ATCC 10231 and
( b ) Aspergillus brasiliensis ATCC 16404. Time to detection (hours) from two independent experiments
is plotted for each fungal concentration (Colony Forming Units).
Reproducibility and Robustness
To evaluate reproducibility and robustness, <100 CFU of the microorganisms specified
in the Ph. Eur. were inoculated into iFA Plus bottles and incubated at 37 → C in six indepen-
dent experiments conducted by different technicians. The mean, standard deviation (SD),
and coefficient of variation (CV) of the TTD were calculated. CV values were below 10%,
as shown in Table 1, except for Cutibacterium acnes . CV ranged from 1.1% for Enterobacter
aerogenes to 13.1% for Cutibacterium acnes .

3.1.3. Effect of Incubation Temperature on Reference Strains
To assess the effect of incubation temperature, <100 CFU of the microorganisms
recommended by Ph. Eur. were inoculated in iFA Plus bottles (aerobic) or iFN Plus bottles
(anaerobic) and incubated at 32 → C and 37 → C. All microorganisms, both bacteria and fungi,
were detected within 3 days, except for Cutibacterium acnes , which required 5.1 days at
37 → C and 6.1 days at 32 → C, as shown in Figure 3.\n\n---\n\n## Page 162\n\nMicroorganisms 2025 , 13 , 2562 8 of 17
